entry.title: A RUN IN THE FIRST, A RUN IN THE SECOND, A RUN IN THE THIRD, AND SEVEN INNINGS OF RASMUSSEN TO KEEP THEM — TWELVE HITS WITHOUT ONE OVER THE WALL MUFFLE THE FOREST CITY NINE, AND THE RAYS CARRY THE AMERICAN QUESTION HOME STANDING ONE VICTORY FROM THE WORLD'S SERIES: RAYS 3, GUARDIANS 1
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 103 · Monday, the Nineteenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

A RUN IN THE FIRST, A RUN IN THE SECOND, A RUN IN THE THIRD, AND SEVEN INNINGS OF RASMUSSEN TO KEEP THEM — TWELVE HITS WITHOUT ONE OVER THE WALL MUFFLE THE FOREST CITY NINE, AND THE RAYS CARRY THE AMERICAN QUESTION HOME STANDING ONE VICTORY FROM THE WORLD'S SERIES: RAYS 3, GUARDIANS 1

Drew Rasmussen holds Cleveland to one run across seven innings on 95 pitches, feeding the left-handed hitters a changeup he did not own a year ago and retiring 14 of 15 men through the middle of the evening; Yandy Díaz opens the proceedings with a double and collects three hits; Jonny DeLuca forces in the first run with a bases-loaded walk that survives Cleveland's appeal to the electronic arbiter, and Jonathan Aranda and Liam Hicks single home the second and third; Steven Kwan throws out one runner at the plate and robs another at the center-field wall in a losing cause; and Bryan Baker closes his sixth spotless errand of the month — the pennant round returns to St. Petersburg with Tampa Bay ahead three games to two

Nobody in a gray uniform struck a ball over a wall at Progressive Field on Sunday night, and nobody needed to. Tampa Bay assembled its three runs the way a clerk assembles a ledger — one entry at a time, each in its proper column — scoring once in each of the first three innings, a thing the franchise had managed in only three previous October contests.5 In the first, Yandy Díaz led off with a double and walked home when Jonny DeLuca, the bases full, declined ball four; Cleveland's catcher Patrick Bailey appealed the call to the league's electronic arbiter, and the machine sided with the walk. In the second, Jonathan Aranda's single to left cashed Ben Williamson; in the third, Liam Hicks dropped a single into center to cash Chandler Simpson. Twelve hits the visitors collected, and only two — doubles by Díaz and Simpson — advanced a man past first base on their own authority; the beaten starter himself certified the method afterward, describing an unselfish nine that shoots the ball through holes rather than swinging for the fences.3 Tyler Wells, who contributed one strikeout to the cause, put it in the house style: "That was Rays baseball at its finest."5

The man guarding the entries was Drew Rasmussen, on the five days' rest this paper noted yesterday he has kept nearly all season: seven innings, four hits, one walk, six strikeouts, 95 pitches. After Chase DeLauter's two-out single in the first he retired nine men running and 14 of the next 15; only six Cleveland balls escaped the infield all evening, a mere three were hard-struck by the measuring instruments' reckoning, and the lone run arrived in the sixth by way of two singles and DeLauter's groundout.4 The quiet work was done by the newest tool in the box — a changeup built only this year, thrown 27 times to Cleveland's left-handed hitters, 28 percent of his pitches and the heaviest he has ever leaned upon it, without surrendering a hit. "It's probably been the single greatest addition I've made to my repertoire in the entirety of my career," said its author; "Three fastballs and a really good changeup," summarized Stephen Vogt, who found no answer to any of the four.4 The October account now reads 21 innings and three runs across three starts: no Tampa Bay pitcher before him had twice gone seven innings allowing one run or none in a postseason, none had strung three quality starts together, and the last man anywhere to bank two such starts before a World's Series was Logan Webb in 2021. Since the All-Star interlude Rasmussen stands 11-0 with a 1.73 earned-run average, 99 strikeouts against 18 walks in 93 2/3 innings, his club winning 14 of those 15 starts — figures that moved Díaz, through the club's interpreter, to a flat verdict: "I really do think he's the best pitcher in MLB."43 Behind him Cam Booser took two outs, Wells one, and Bryan Baker worked a clean ninth for his fifth save — six errands this October, no runs, one hit allowed in the whole of them, company kept only by Jason Motte and Mark Wohlers among pitchers who finished each of their first six postseason appearances.5

The defeat was not for want of gallantry. Steven Kwan, having judged his own second-inning throw insufficient, atoned in the fourth: he gathered Aranda's single in left and cut down Taylor Walls at the plate on one true bounce to Bailey — "off the bat, I thought there was no chance of a play," admitted Kevin Cash — and in the ninth, shifted to center field, he leapt at the wall to strip Victor Mesa Jr. of extra bases. "I was glad to save some runs there, but I left some meat on the bone, I felt like, with that first one," was the Gold Glove man's own accounting. José Ramírez added a barehanded pickup of Simpson's eighth-inning bunt, and Vogt spoke the epitaph: "That game could have looked a lot different without our defense tonight."6 True, and insufficient — for the deeper wound was the start. Parker Messick, moved up a game by the rainout's arithmetic as this paper set out Sunday, lasted two innings, the shortest start of his career, on 57 laboring pitches; his season's account now stands at exactly 200 innings against a previous professional high of 138 1/3, and the workload question the Herald carried yesterday morning answered itself by the third inning.7 Tampa Bay's leather answered Cleveland's besides: Williamson dove to rob Ramírez in the fourth, and Walls — "one of the best shortstops on the planet," per the opposing manager — spun in the grass behind second to end the fifth.5

So the scholars' arithmetic this paper offered Cleveland as comfort only yesterday changes its allegiance: in series knotted at two games apiece, the fifth game's winner has taken the argument in 46 cases of 69, and road winners of such fifth games in 21 of 28.3 Tampa Bay flies home wanting one victory for the third World's Series in franchise history, the visits of 2008 and 2020 having both ended in defeat — and should the Rays take it, the 122nd Series is guaranteed a first-time champion, for neither they nor the waiting Brewers have ever won one. Cleveland, whose 77 seasons without a title since 1948 stand as the game's longest sorrow, must now win twice in two nights on foreign carpet; "We need to rebound tomorrow," said Vogt, master of the available options.3 The 36,303 by the lake filed out quietly after 2 hours and 50 minutes of clear, 63-degree October. The dome tonight will be louder — the particulars of the sixth game are set out at the Elimination Desk below.

News Around the League

THE ELIMINATION DESK: PERALTA, SIX VICTORIES WITHOUT A DEFEAT AND AN 0.79 FIGURE SINCE THE SIX-AND-TWENTIETH OF AUGUST, TAKES THE BALL UNDER THE DOME TONIGHT — CLEVELAND ANSWERS BY COMMITTEE WITH WILLIAMS HELD FOR A SEVENTH GAME IT MUST FIRST EARN, AND THE TROP AWAITS THE FIRST PENNANT EVER CLINCHED ON ITS CARPET

The sixth game goes tonight at 8:08 at Tropicana Field, and the pitching ledgers could scarcely sit further apart. Tampa Bay hands the ball to Freddy Peralta — 10-11 with a 4.42 for the whole of his itinerant season, but 6-0 with a 0.79 earned-run average over nine appearances since August 26, including a 0.99 figure with 26 strikeouts across five starts under this very dome — fresh from six shutout innings in the second game and the two borrowed relief outs in the fourth that this paper recorded in its Sunday number.8 Cleveland must stitch its evening from the committee: Slade Cecconi may open, with Tanner Bibee — one-third of an inning pitched all month — and Joey Cantillo expected to carry roughly two innings apiece, the high-leverage men behind them. Gavin Williams, the round's great strikeout engine, is barred on short rest — "No, that's not an option," said Stephen Vogt, whose ace's fastball sagged from 99.2 to 95.4 miles the hour across five innings of the third game — and Foster Griffin and Parker Messick are both spent, so Williams waits instead upon a Tuesday seventh game his club must first earn.78 The committee's spokesman kept it short: "It's crunch time," said Cecconi. "Whatever they need, I'm ready for."7

The stage carries its own story. Tropicana Field, shuttered by Hurricane Milton two Octobers ago while the club kept house elsewhere, returned this season to harbor a 55-26 home campaign — the best in the game, jointly with Milwaukee's — and has yielded three victories in four postseason sittings; no Tampa Bay pennant has ever been clinched upon its carpet, the 2020 flag having been won as the home club of a neutral yard.10 Cleveland, for its part, has been in this hole before and climbed out — down two games to none against the White Sox only a round ago — and its manager declines all despair: "This is when this team thrives," says Vogt, and "if there's a group I'm betting on to get this done, it's our guys."78

THE PROCLAMATION DESK: 'WE'RE GOING TO WIN TOMORROW' — DÍAZ, FIVE HITS IN TWO NIGHTS AND THE LAST MAN STANDING FROM THE 2020 PENNANT-WINNERS, DECLARES THE ROUND CONCLUDED, WHILE THE CLEVELAND BATS HAVE MANAGED FOUR RUNS SINCE HALPIN'S WALLOP

Guarantees are rare currency in October, where the game collects its debts promptly, but Yandy Díaz issued one Sunday night with the serenity of a man reading from a bank book. "It's a great opportunity. All of us are thinking of it," the 35-year-old said of the pennant through the club's interpreter — "But it all ends tomorrow. We're going to win tomorrow."9 The affidavit behind the boast is in order: three hits Sunday atop two Saturday, safe arrival in seven of his eight October contests, and a leadoff post from which, in his manager Kevin Cash's four words, "He goes, we go." The longer ledger is in order too — the only man on the active roster remaining from the 2020 pennant-winners has now played 33 postseason games in a Tampa Bay uniform, more than any man in franchise history, and his 25 postseason hits trail only Randy Arozarena's 38 and B.J. Upton's 27 on the club's all-time roll, all atop a season of .293, 22 home runs and 85 driven in across a career-high 154 games.9

The men he proposes to dismiss are, at present, struggling to furnish a rebuttal. Since Petey Halpin's bat-flipping blow turned the third game — the high-water mark of Cleveland's October, as readers of this paper's Friday number will recall — the Cleveland bats have produced four runs in two games, yesterday's lone tally arriving on a groundout; the club neither leaves the yard nor manufactures by other means, and the round has tilted accordingly.10 Their manager's answer to the guarantee was not a counter-boast but a position report: "We don't have another choice."9

THE PROPRIETOR'S DESK: 'YOU WON'T BE SO CHEERY WHEN YOU LOSE FOR ANOTHER TWO-AND-TWENTY YEARS,' A RETIRED SCRIBE TOLD ATTANASIO AT HIS FIRST MILWAUKEE INTERVIEW IN 2004 — TWO-AND-TWENTY YEARS LATER, TO THE AUTUMN, THE MAN HOLDS A PENNANT

When Mark Attanasio was introduced as the Brewers' new owner on October 4, 2004, a long-retired reporter in the front row of his first media scrum offered a prophecy: "You won't be so cheery when you lose for another 22 years!" Twenty-two years had then passed since Milwaukee's only World's Series appearance, in 1982. Twenty-two years later, to the very autumn, Attanasio stood on the Dodger Stadium grass while his club celebrated a pennant, and permitted himself the obvious arithmetic: "Here we are, 22 years later."11

The intervening ledger rewards inspection. The front office he purchased counted about 130 full-time souls; it now counts more than 400. His first club played to .500 — Milwaukee's first non-losing season in 13 years — a 26-year postseason famine ended in 2008, and the last nine seasons have brought eight Octobers, six division flags and three pennant rounds, culminating in this year's franchise-record 103 victories and an 18-6 September.11 The owner confesses the summit frightened him more than the climb: "I was more nervous than I have ever been because this could actually happen," he said of the fourth game. "It's the first time I felt pressure — real pressure. And fortunately, our guys delivered." His president of business operations, the Milwaukee-born Rick Schlesinger, supplied the creed of the regime — ownership as "a public trust," the club "really, effectively, owned by the fans" and Attanasio its steward — and the Herald, which keeps a skeptical eye on the proprietor class as a body, notes without irony that this is precisely the manner of stewardship it recommends to the other 29.11

THE APPRENTICE DESK: 'WE HIT UNTIL OUR HANDS WERE BLEEDING' — PRATT, A SHORTSTOP OF TWO-AND-TWENTY RAISED ON NIGHTLY BATTING IN A MISSISSIPPI YARD, CARRIES A .310 OCTOBER INTO THE WORLD'S SERIES

The pennant-winners' shortstop is a rookie who turned 22 during his first big-league season and plays the position as though he has held it for a decade. Cooper Pratt batted .281 with a .350 on-base mark across 74 games after his summons to Milwaukee, and has raised the figure to .310 through the club's October — an apprenticeship conducted in the loudest classrooms the game offers.12

The making of him was nightly and unglamorous. His father Russell, a college player at Utah who runs a youth baseball concern in northern Mississippi, had Cooper and his elder brother Ozzie — later of Ole Miss — hitting nearly every evening, no days off granted or requested. "We hit until our hands were bleeding," the young man reports, adding with candor, "I hated it for the longest time." His mother Heidi played college softball before becoming a family physician; the household's verdict on his temperament is unanimous. "He's so level, so steady. Never too up, never too down," says the father. Milwaukee took him in the sixth round of the 2023 draft and paid above the slot to sign him, and its infield coach Matt Erickson now suspects "a really high ceiling as a defender that maybe he didn't even know about." The apprentice's own summation wants no ornament: "This has always been my dream."12

The forward ledger is one line with a continent of weight in it: the sixth game of the American round tonight at 8:08 under the dome at St. Petersburg, a seventh there Tuesday only if Cleveland insists, and the World's Series opening Friday, the 23rd, at Milwaukee against whichever club survives.2 One side has promised the matter concluded; the other climbed out of this same hole only a round ago. The Herald ventures no guarantee of its own save the standing one — that tomorrow's number will carry the full account, pennant or stay of execution. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: TWO HUNDRED SIXTY-FOUR SUCH BLOWS HAD ALWAYS LEFT THE YARD, AND THE TWO HUNDRED SIXTY-FIFTH DIED IN HALPIN'S GLOVE — YET CAMINERO AND HIS FELLOWS WOULD NOT BE REFUSED, AND THE AMERICAN QUESTION STANDS LEVEL AT TWO GAMES APIECE: RAYS 7, GUARDIANS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 102 · Sunday, the Eighteenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

TWO HUNDRED SIXTY-FOUR SUCH BLOWS HAD ALWAYS LEFT THE YARD, AND THE TWO HUNDRED SIXTY-FIFTH DIED IN HALPIN'S GLOVE — YET CAMINERO AND HIS FELLOWS WOULD NOT BE REFUSED, AND THE AMERICAN QUESTION STANDS LEVEL AT TWO GAMES APIECE: RAYS 7, GUARDIANS 3

Petey Halpin crashes into the center-field wall to rob Junior Caminero of a drive that, by the ledger of every like ball struck since the measuring instruments went up, had never once stayed in a ballpark — and Caminero answers two innings later with the go-ahead double anyway; Jonathan Aranda, hitless in ten tries entering the night, collects three hits and two runs batted in; Yandy Díaz closes the account with a two-run homer to the opposite field in the ninth; and Nick Martinez's 5 1/3 innings of one-run ball, preserved by two borrowed outs from Freddy Peralta, square the pennant round and guarantee its return to St. Petersburg on Monday

Begin with the cruelest out of the month. In the fourth inning Saturday night at Progressive Field, Junior Caminero struck a ball 110.7 miles the hour at the sweet-spot angle — and since the league's measuring instruments began their ledger in 2015, 264 balls had been hit so, and all 264 were home runs. The 265th hung in the frigid lakefront air nearly six full seconds while Petey Halpin ran a crooked, backpedaling errand to the deepest corner of center field, gathered it at the base of the wall, and struck the barrier with a thud the yard heard twice over. "For that to stay in the yard, it's got to do some funky stuff," said the robbed man's robber; "100%," said Caminero, asked if he thought it gone.7 Foster Griffin, who threw the pitch, called the play unbelievable and the ball a home run in any number of other parks.7

Cleveland's luck, having spent itself so extravagantly on one catch, ran dry thereafter. Caminero returned in the sixth and laced Daniel Espino's offering 110.2 miles the hour over the leaping José Ramírez into the left-field corner, cashing Jonathan Aranda for the lead, then stood atop second base in his October layers beating his chest at his own dugout.34 It was the awakening the Rays had waited a round for. Their celebrated top three — Díaz, Aranda and Caminero, whom the manager Kevin Cash needles in lean weeks as los tres pequeños, the three little ones — had come to Cleveland a combined 5-for-34 with one run batted in and 13 strikeouts; on Saturday they went 6-for-14 and drove in five. Aranda, hitless in the series at nightfall, finished 3-for-4; Díaz doubled, then sealed the business in the ninth with a two-run homer carried just over the right-field wall, opposite-field work of the barrel-chested old school.43 "It was just a matter of time for us three to get going," said Aranda through the club's interpreter.4

The pitching held up its end with room to spare. Nick Martinez, 36 years of age and master of three fastballs and a changeup he refused to abandon after spiking it early, allowed Steven Kwan's first-inning single and Chase DeLauter's run-scoring knock — DeLauter promptly cut down stretching for two by Victor Mesa Jr.'s sliding stop and throw — and then retired 11 men in succession, handing over 5 1/3 innings of one-run ball and collecting the first postseason victory of his long career. "He did a lot of Nick things out there," certified Cash.5 When Martinez departed with a man aboard in the sixth, the relief was Freddy Peralta — the Game 2 starter, lately of the Mets, whose between-starts throw-day the Rays simply relocated from the bullpen mound to the sixth inning of a pennant round. He recorded his two outs and kept the lead at one. "I'm just a reliever," he teased the writers afterward. "Why do you want to talk to me?" His starter answered for them: "He saved our game today."6

The seventh settled it, and unkindly for the home nine. Richie Palacios and Taylor Walls scored on Aranda's single to right, which skipped under DeLauter's glove for two bases more and an unearned third run when Chandler Simpson's sacrifice fly followed. "Put that one on me," said DeLauter, declining every excuse offered him. "You miss a ground ball and give up two runs — essentially give up three."11 Cleveland answered gamely — Travis Bazzana's first postseason homer and Brayan Rocchio's run-scoring single made it 5-3, and Kwan finished the evening with gauze packed in a lip he split diving into first base — but no nearer.8 So the round stands two games apiece, a best-of-three with the home dome recovered: the fifth game goes this very evening at five o'clock by the lake, Drew Rasmussen against the rookie Parker Messick, and the sixth is now guaranteed for Monday night at St. Petersburg.32 The scholars' comfort for Cleveland, who stood one swing from a three-games-to-one grip: in series knotted at two, the fifth game's winner has taken the argument in 46 cases of 69.8 The 33,355 who sat through 46 degrees of partly cloudy went home with the same arithmetic.1

News Around the League

THE PIVOT DESK: THE FIFTH GAME GOES AT FIVE O'CLOCK THIS EVENING, AND THE RAINOUT'S STRANGE GIFTS ARE NOW PLAIN — RASMUSSEN ON HIS ACCUSTOMED FIFTH DAY AGAINST MESSICK MOVED UP A GAME, WITH A PENNANT'S WORTH OF LEVERAGE ON THE TABLE

Friday's washout, which this paper mourned at the time, has proved an even-handed quartermaster. Drew Rasmussen takes the ball for Tampa Bay tonight on the five days' rest he kept nearly all season — his October account stands at 14 innings, two runs, two walks and 17 strikeouts across two starts, atop a 16-5, 2.67 regular campaign — while Cleveland, as this paper supposed yesterday it might, moves Parker Messick up from his appointed sixth game to the fifth, on normal rest, precisely because the postponement shoved the calendar a day.1081 The rookie left-hander's season now runs to 198 innings, the sixth-most by a first-year man in the last 20 years and far past his previous high of 138 1/3; his manager has allowed that some October command trouble may be the workload talking. The rookie himself files no grievance: "Honestly, my body feels great. To be able to take the ball in this game shows the confidence the team has in me."98

The stakes require no embroidery: the winner flies to St. Petersburg tonight holding three games of the four won and one victory from the World's Series; the loser bats for his life Monday. Cleveland's manager Stephen Vogt declares himself unshaken — "I'll put our guys up against any team in the world in a three-game series" — and holds in reserve a rested late guard of Hunter Gaddis, Erik Sabrowski and Cade Smith, none of whom worked in Saturday's seven-man bullpen procession.108 Tampa Bay, for its part, wanted exactly this: "That was one of the main objectives that we had here coming into Cleveland, just to force the series back home," said Jonathan Aranda. The forecast, for once, has nothing to say: clear and cold by the lake.10

THE WAITING DESK: SEVEN FULL DAYS OF IDLENESS FOR THE PENNANT-HOLDERS, THE LONGEST SIT OF ANY FLAG-WINNER SAVE THE '07 ROCKIES — AND THE LEDGER ON LONG RESTS READS EXACTLY EVEN, THOUGH THE RECENT PAGES LEAN AGAINST THE RESTED

Milwaukee's reward for sweeping its round by Thursday is a week of waiting: seven full days between the pennant and Friday's first game of the World's Series, the club's longest pause since spring training and the second-longest any flag-winner has endured since the championship rounds went to seven games in 1985. Only the 2007 Rockies sat longer — eight days, after winning 21 of 22 — and they were promptly swept by Boston, a precedent Milwaukee is free to decline.12

The full accounting is studiedly neutral. Since the postseason took its three-round shape in 1995, clubs entering the Series with the extra rest stand exactly 15-15; clubs that sat five full days or more, as the Brewers will, went 10-10. But the recent pages lean the other way — since 2009 the club that clinched its pennant first has gone 4-12 in the Series, and from 2009 through 2017 the less-rested club won nine straight.12 The sweep itself cuts both ways: of the 11 previous clubs that reached the Series by sweeping a seven-game round, only four finished the job — though the three most recent of them, the 2019 Nationals, 2022 Astros and 2025 Dodgers, all did.12 The Suds men may prefer the simplest reading: the first game goes Friday evening at their own yard, and nobody idle has lost anything yet.122

THE SHORTSTOP DESK: DOMBROWSKI SERVES NOTICE ON HIS $300 MILLION MAN — MEND THE GLOVE BY SPRING OR QUIT THE POSITION, PHILADELPHIA TELLS TURNER, AFTER A SEASON OF ONE-AND-TWENTY ERRORS

The bluntest sentence of the young offseason was pronounced in Philadelphia. Dave Dombrowski, the Quakers' president of baseball operations, summoned Trea Turner to Citizens Bank Park on Tuesday and told the shortstop — seven years and $190 million still owed on his $300 million engagement — that his defense must recover or his position will. "He knows he has to be better at shortstop," Dombrowski reported. "I told him it's really mandatory that it's like that. You cannot play shortstop like you did defensively in '26 going to '27."13

The indictment is in the ledger: Turner, 33, batted .242 with a .675 on-base-plus-slugging — perhaps the worst season of his career — and committed 21 errors at shortstop, the most in the league, before going 1-for-11 in the Wild Card defeat at Atlanta's hands. The remedies sketched are several: Turner to the outfield, which he does not prefer; Bryson Stott across the bag to shortstop; the prospect Aidan Miller, recovered from a year lost to his back, competing for a place by spring. Turner, to his credit, filed no appeal — "I've got a lot of work to do," he said. "Find answers. See what I did bad."13 The man's no-trade clause makes him all but immovable, so the parties are wedded to the repair — and with a work stoppage reckoned all but certain come December, the winter may afford him more drilling time than anyone would wish.13 The Herald, whose sympathies in such matters are on record, merely notes that a club which can owe one workman $190 million has settled the question of whether the till is empty.

THE AUCTION DESK: THE WINTER MARKET'S CROWN LOT IS ALREADY POSTED — SKUBAL, RENTED BY LOS ANGELES AT THE COST OF TWO PROSPECTS OF THE FIRST RANK, NOW STANDS TO COMMAND THE RICHEST PITCHING CONTRACT EVER LET

The Dodgers' early exit opens the bidding season, and the first lot is the grandest. Tarik Skubal heads a class of nine Los Angeles free agents — Kiké Hernández, Evan Phillips, Alex Vesia, Blake Treinen and the retiring Miguel Rojas among the others — and is reckoned the top player on the whole market. Los Angeles paid dearly for its three months of him at the summer deadline: the ready-made starter River Ryan, the outfield prospect Zyhir Hope and the right-hander Brady Smith, all to Detroit, for a rental now concluded.14

The walk-year ledger holds up its end. Skubal went 12-7 with a 2.72 earned-run average across 26 starts split between the Tigers and Dodgers, despite six weeks lost to a left elbow operation; last winter he took a record $32 million from Detroit in the arbitration room — an award this desk files among the honest victories of the workingman's side of the ledger — and he is now widely expected to surpass Yoshinobu Yamamoto's twelve-year, $325 million engagement as the largest guarantee ever extended a pitcher.14 Whether Los Angeles, which must also weigh the futures of its own young men, re-enters the bidding for the man it rented is the question Chavez Ravine will chew on all winter; the pitcher himself, asked after Thursday's elimination, preferred not to discuss it.14

The forward ledger is brief and loud: the fifth game of the American round this evening at five o'clock by the lake, the sixth Monday night at St. Petersburg, and a seventh Tuesday at the same address only if the argument insists; the World's Series opens Friday, the 23rd, at Milwaukee, where the hosts wait out the week in enforced leisure.2 By tomorrow's number one club will stand a single victory from the pennant, and the other will be rehearsing arguments for a Monday jury. The Herald will be at its post for all of it. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Postseason Off-Day Edition — the Seventeenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 101 · Saturday, the Seventeenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the pennant races rest.

0 days until the fourth game of the American League's pennant round — the Rays at the Guardians, eight o'clock this very evening by the lake (Saturday, the 17th of October, 2026).

News Around the League

THE TARPAULIN DESK: THE SKY HOLDS ITS VETO OVER THE LAKE AND THE FOURTH GAME NEVER THROWS A PITCH — THE AMERICAN ROUND MOVES WHOLESALE TO TONIGHT AT EIGHT, SUNDAY SURRENDERS ITS DAY OF REST, AND THE DOME STANDS BY FOR MONDAY

The washout this paper feared only yesterday arrived on schedule and stayed past all bargaining. Rain settled over Progressive Field through Friday afternoon and declined every invitation to leave; the grounds crew swept standing water from the infield tarpaulin and chased the pools collecting on the warning track; a party of Tampa Bay pitchers emerged to play catch near the appointed hour and promptly thought better of it; and late in the evening the league called the thing off. "It never cleared out the way they were hoping it would," said Kevin Cash, who allowed that the league and both clubs "did everything they could to try to get it in." His opposite number took the longer view of local meteorology. "This is baseball. This is Cleveland," said Stephen Vogt. "We're more than used to these kinds of days."3

The week is accordingly redrawn, precisely as this paper warned it might be. The fourth game goes tonight at eight o'clock by the lake; the fifth follows Sunday at five o'clock, the scheduled day of rest stricken from the calendar; and should the argument require a sixth and a seventh, they wait at the Gulf Coast dome Monday and Tuesday nights.36 The standing of the quarrel is untouched by weather: the Lake Erie men lead it two games to one and may yet take the pennant without packing a trunk, while the Tampa men must win three of the four that remain. Even the ticket desk is shuffled with the games — Friday's stubs are good for Sunday, and Saturday's stand exactly where they are. The forecast, for its part, has repented: nothing heavier than ordinary October is projected tonight, the thermometer bound for 40 degrees by the late innings.3

THE CHESSBOARD DESK: A FREE DAY TO RESHUFFLE AND NEITHER MANAGER TOUCHES A PIECE — MARTINEZ KEEPS THE BALL FOR TAMPA BAY, ARMSTRONG STILL OPENS FOR CLEVELAND, AND THE TRUE MANEUVERING IS SAVED FOR SUNDAY

A postponement hands each side the rarest October commodity — choice — and both clubs promptly declined it. Nick Martinez, 15-6 with a 3.10 mark on the year, takes the ball tonight for the Gulf Coast club exactly as he would have Friday, and Cash would commit to nothing beyond him: "We'll go day to day from there." The logic wants little defending. Martinez has thrown 13 scoreless innings against these same Guardians over two regular-season meetings; his 2.38 figure on the road stood fourth in the American League — behind a list that includes, pointedly, Cleveland's own Parker Messick — and the Rays have gone 23-9 when he starts. "Nick's been a leader for us all year. He's been the bridge that's held us together," says Chandler Simpson. "When he's on the mound, we know our leader's on the mound."4

The deferred riches come later. Drew Rasmussen — worked hard of late, with a career-high 114 pitches in his final regular-season turn and better than 90 in each of two October starts since — now lines up for Sunday's fifth game on the five days' rest he kept nearly all season, and Freddy Peralta, warm off his Game 2 gem, stands ready for a sixth game should the series reach the dome.4 Cleveland's answer is the bullpen day it had long pencilled in for this spot: Shawn Armstrong, 2-1 with a 4.58 mark, opens — "Armstrong's going to start for us tomorrow," said Vogt on Friday night, and then said it again, in the manner of a man closing a subject — with Foster Griffin rested and unnamed but conspicuously available for the bulk innings behind him, and Tanner Bibee, Joey Cantillo and Slade Cecconi all in reserve. The rookie Messick, who started the second game, could move up to Sunday, when a pennant may sit on the table.5 And the idle Friday fattened both bullpens — no small mercy for the Lake Erie men, who have ridden Cade Smith and Hunter Gaddis hard through the month.3

THE HOMEFRONT DESK: THE CREAM CITY REARRANGES ITSELF AROUND FRIDAY — THE BASKETBALL CLUB MOVES ITS OPENING NIGHT TO MID-AFTERNOON FOR GAME ONE OF THE 122ND WORLD'S SERIES, AND THE FOOTBALL COACH TURNS UP IN A BREWERS CAP

Milwaukee's first World's Series since 1982 opens Friday next, the 23rd of October, at American Family Field — the first game of the 122nd Fall Classic, the National League's champion hosting whichever club survives the week by the lake — and the city has begun clearing its calendar accordingly.62 The Bucks, the town's basketball concern, were booked to raise the curtain on their own season at the Fiserv Forum that very evening; the club and its league have moved the tip-off from seven o'clock to three, "in recognition of this historic occasion," so that no Milwaukeean need choose between openings.7

"The Brewers' return to the World Series for the first time in 44 years is a special moment for Milwaukee and sports fans across Wisconsin," the basketball men declared, promising to cheer the baseball club from down the street. And up the road in Green Bay, Matt LaFleur, who coaches the football eleven, took Friday's press conference in a Brewers cap. "I want to support the Brewers," he said. "That was pretty cool to watch last night."7 The Suds men themselves, swept to the pennant and idle until their opponent is named, can only watch the lake with the rest of us.

THE TWO-WAY DESK: 'YES, DEFINITELY' — OHTANI, SILENT ON THE MOUND SINCE THE THIRD OF JULY, VOWS TO PITCH IN 2027, THOUGH WHETHER THE WINTER INCLUDES THE SURGEONS IS A QUESTION HE LEAVES OPEN

Shohei Ohtani's season ended Thursday night in the on-deck circle, bat in hand, and his first public business of the offseason was to promise both halves of himself back. Asked after the Angelenos' season-closing 6-4 defeat whether he means to pitch next year, the four-time Most Valuable answered through his interpreter without a comma's hesitation: "Yes, definitely. And looking forward to having a better season next year." Whether the road back runs through an operating theater is not yet settled — "hard to tell at this point," he allowed; it is "something that's going to be analyzed, discussed over the offseason."8

The mound half of him was, while it lasted, superb: a 1.79 earned-run average and a .179 mark against across 85 2/3 innings. But the left knee began complaining on June 11, the final four starts leaked 12 earned runs in 24 2/3 innings where all the work before had allowed 5 in 61, and after the third of July he did not pitch again — a September fortnight on the injured list for the right biceps, his first such visit in nearly three years, closing the ledger. This paper carried his insistence Wednesday that he could help with the bat regardless, and he did, the three-run homer in Thursday's finale ending a drought of two months. The career figures explain the stubbornness: among starters with 500 innings pitched since 1969, only Jim Palmer, Jacob deGrom and Clayton Kershaw own a better earned-run average than his 2.83.8

THE LEATHER DESK: THE SHAKIEST GLOVE OF 2025 IS A FINALIST FOR THE GOLD OF 2026 — SIMPSON LEARNS OF HIS NOMINATION FROM HIS OWN TELEPHONE IN A CLEVELAND HOTEL, AND THE COACH WHO REBUILT HIM SHARES THE CREDIT

The Rawlings nominations this paper recorded Thursday carried one story worth telling on its own. Chandler Simpson, the Rays' left fielder, woke in his Cleveland hotel Wednesday, took up his telephone for the morning's idle scrolling, and found himself tagged in congratulations: a Gold Glove finalist, alongside Cody Bellinger of the Yankees and Wyatt Langford of the Rangers, the verdicts sealed until the first of November. "Oh, wow," the 25-year-old reports thinking. "OK, cool."9

The arithmetic of the conversion is the story. A year ago the league's accounting had Simpson at minus-5 outs above average, the 11th percentile of all defenders; this season he stands at plus-8, the 93rd, and the runs-saved ledger swung from minus-9 to plus-8. The credit is shared, by every account including the manager's, with Corey Dickerson, the first-base coach and former outfielder whose daily instruction taught the fastest man in the league to read the ball off the bat and stand where it was going. "I think that is maybe one of the coolest stories of our season, where he was defensively last year, where he's come to this year," said Cash.9 Nor is the glove the whole of the tale: when Friday's rained-out lineup was posted, Simpson stood third in the batting order — contact and speed deployed where sluggers ordinarily reside — and the assignment is expected to survive to tonight.3

October has now emptied three Fridays running — twice by the bracket's own design, and last night by the sky's veto. What remains is simply told: the American question resumes tonight at eight by the lake, continues Sunday at five with no day of rest between, and removes to the Gulf Coast dome Monday and Tuesday only if Tampa Bay makes it necessary; Milwaukee waits on the far side with Friday's curtain already hung.36 A pennant may be had by Sunday evening, or the argument may run the whole week — either way the Herald will be at its post with the full account. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE LAST BALL OF THE NATIONAL LEAGUE'S YEAR COMES DOWN IN CHOURIO'S GLOVE — DOWN FOUR RUNS BEFORE THE SECOND INNING HAD COOLED, THE BREWERS CLIMB OUT A SIXTH TIME THIS OCTOBER, SWEEP THE TWICE-CROWNED CHAMPIONS FROM THEIR OWN YARD, AND CARRY MILWAUKEE TO ITS FIRST WORLD'S SERIES SINCE 1982: BREWERS 6, DODGERS 4
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 100 · Friday, the Sixteenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 2 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE LAST BALL OF THE NATIONAL LEAGUE'S YEAR COMES DOWN IN CHOURIO'S GLOVE — DOWN FOUR RUNS BEFORE THE SECOND INNING HAD COOLED, THE BREWERS CLIMB OUT A SIXTH TIME THIS OCTOBER, SWEEP THE TWICE-CROWNED CHAMPIONS FROM THEIR OWN YARD, AND CARRY MILWAUKEE TO ITS FIRST WORLD'S SERIES SINCE 1982: BREWERS 6, DODGERS 4

Shohei Ohtani's three-run homer — his first in two months, ending the longest drought of his career — stakes Los Angeles to a 4-0 lead in the second inning, and Milwaukee answers the way it has answered all month: back-to-back doubles from William Contreras and Jake Bauers, a bases-loaded walk, Garrett Mitchell's go-ahead drive in the sixth and David Hamilton's parting shot in the ninth, while Aaron Ashby records the final nine outs; no club had ever erased a four-run deficit to finish a postseason sweep, and no club had ever been swept by an opponent one October and swept that same opponent the next

The National League's season ended in the glove of Jackson Chourio, on a fly ball that died just short of the left-center warning track at Dodger Stadium on Thursday night, and the noise that followed belonged to the visitors' dugout and to the several thousand Wisconsinites among the 49,104 who declined to go home. They stayed to watch the Warren C. Giles Trophy presented on enemy ground, and they were entitled: Milwaukee has waited 44 years for this, since the 1982 club of Harvey's Wallbangers carried the American League's flag and lost a seven-game World's Series to St. Louis. This pennant is the franchise's first in the National League — and the cry of that earlier October, "Milwaukee, you have a World Series!", belonged by the record not to Bob Uecker but to his partner Dwayne Mosley, Uecker having slipped down to the clubhouse to ready the celebration broadcast. The city may now compose a new one.43

The evening began as the champions' best of the month. Shane Drohan opened for Milwaukee and walked two; Dustin May inherited the second inning and absorbed four runs of it — Andy Pages' single for the first, and then Shohei Ohtani, restored to the leadoff post he had not occupied since September 27, turning a 1-1 cutter into a three-run drive to right-center. It was Ohtani's first home run since August 18, the end of a 115-plate-appearance drought, the longest of his career, whose every barren week this paper has chronicled.38 From 4-0 the ledger turned by installments. Contreras and Bauers struck back-to-back doubles in the fourth, Bauers' a ground-rule bounce worth two runs; in the fifth David Hamilton singled home Sal Frelick and Bauers drew a bases-loaded walk for the tie; in the sixth Garrett Mitchell led off against the left-hander Tanner Scott and hit the go-ahead homer to center; and in the ninth Hamilton — the nine-hole man, two hits, two runs driven in and a stolen base on his evening — added a parting shot off Edwin Díaz's hanging slider.3

The final nine outs belonged to Aaron Ashby, on 39 pitches, and they were not uneventful: he stranded the tying run in scoring position in both the seventh and the eighth, striking out Ohtani swinging with that run at third base. The save ran three full innings in a pennant-clincher, company he shares with only Lance McCullers Jr., Madison Bumgarner, Steve Howe and Vida Blue since the save became an official statistic in 1969; his October account now shows 12 1/3 innings and no runs across six errands.87 The relief corps as a body allowed five runs in 21 2/3 innings of the round, a 2.08 figure, and Joel Romero's victory Thursday meant a reliever won all four games of the series — a thing no best-of-seven sweep had ever shown — and seven of Milwaukee's eight games this postseason, which no club had done either.75

Mitchell's blow deserves its biography. Diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes at nine years old, he slid to the 20th selection of his draft on the doubts that diagnosis bred, wears an insulin pod wired to his telephone, and has played more games this season than in his first four years combined. On Wednesday he and Bauers struck back-to-back homers off a left-hander — lefty upon lefty, a sequence only Ruth and Gehrig in 1928 and Schwarber and Harper earlier this very month had written before them — and on Thursday he supplied the pennant's deciding run. "It was time to make the big shift," said his father Antony, who reports that his son has always run on doubt as other men run on praise.6

The ledger of the series reads like a page from the game's far shelf. The four-run recovery is the largest ever to finish a postseason sweep, and ties the largest in any pennant-clinching game since the rounds began in 1969, matching the Yankees of 2000 and 2003; Milwaukee trailed in all four games of a series it swept, which no club had done; its six comeback victories in its first eight October games stand alone in the records.5 The Brewers are the fifth club to sweep a reigning champion from a best-of-seven — after the 1990 Reds, 1966 Orioles, 1963 Dodgers and 1914 Braves, every one of whom went on to the World's Series — and the first ever, in this sport, to be swept by an opponent one postseason and sweep that same opponent whole the next, the wound of last year's four-game dismissal at these same hands repaid to the penny. This was the 11th best-of-seven ever played between two 100-win clubs and the first to end in a sweep, and Los Angeles even lost its first October game of the year with Tyler Glasnow pitching, a distinction the man had carried through seven appearances.53 The valedictories were brief. "We got outplayed in all facets," said Dave Roberts. "You remember it," said Pat Murphy of the beatings his club once took in this yard. "You have to have that faith," said the captain Christian Yelich, "and you have to have, like, the belief that you know this group can get it done."34 The World's Series opens Friday next, October 23, at American Family Field, against the winner of the American round — whose state of play the Postseason Card takes up below.142

The Postseason Card

THE EIGHTH MAN IN THE ORDER SENDS HIS BAT SKYWARD AND THE BALL TO THE BLEACHERS — HALPIN'S TWO-RUN WALLOP OVERTURNS AN AFTERNOON SIMPSON'S TRIPLE HAD BRIEFLY STOLEN, WILLIAMS FANS NINE MORE IN FIVE, AND THE CLEVELAND NINE STAND TWO WINS FROM THE WORLD'S SERIES: GUARDIANS 3, RAYS 2

October baseball by daylight, at the one-o'clock hour the rain dictated, and 30,101 fill the lakefront yard anyway; Gavin Williams strikes out nine of the eighteen men he faces and departs early by design, Chandler Simpson's two-strike triple gives Tampa Bay a short-lived lead, and Petey Halpin — a reserve outfielder a fortnight ago — answers with a two-run homer off Griffin Jax and a bat flip his own bullpen scored a ten, before Cade Smith's four-out save sends Cleveland ahead two games to one

The afternoon appointment this paper commended yesterday to readers of flexible luncheon arrangements proved worth the leave-taking. Under a sunny 62 degrees at Progressive Field — the one-o'clock start having been dictated by the evening's forecast — 30,101 turned out on a weekday midday and were repaid in two hours and twenty-eight minutes. Cleveland struck first in the second, Nathaniel Lowe lining a double to right to cash Jo Adell; Tampa Bay answered in the fourth when Chandler Simpson, down to his last strike, lashed a two-run triple past Chase DeLauter to score Yandy Díaz and Victor Mesa Jr. — the speedster's third run driven in of the round, and very nearly the whole of the visitors' offense.10

The reply came from the eighth place in the order. Patrick Bailey singled with one out in the fifth, and Petey Halpin — until a fortnight ago a late-innings defensive reserve, pressed into the lineup in the Chicago round and never since removed — turned Griffin Jax's 96-mile sinker into the right-field bleachers, 105 off the bat, for the lead. The bat went skyward in a high, turning arc. "I just kind of blacked out," Halpin pleaded afterward — October's fashionable alibi, Jake Bauers having entered the same one at the dome on Monday. "It was majestic," certified Steven Kwan; Daniel Espino, warming in the bullpen, scored the flip a ten while confessing he feared the lumber might strike its owner on the way down.11

Gavin Williams made the two runs stand. Five innings, two hits, nine strikeouts — both runs rode Simpson's triple — and a departure at 70 pitches that his manager called precaution rather than necessity. The figures behind the figures: 33 strikeouts in 16 2/3 innings this October, a 45.9 percent strikeout rate that is the highest any pitcher has carried through a postseason of ten innings or more, past Corey Knebel's 44.6; no Cleveland pitcher before him had struck out nine or better in three straight postseason starts; and his 45 October strikeouts for the franchise passed Andrew Miller for fourth on the all-time roll, behind Charles Nagy's 55, Orel Hershiser's 54 and Corey Kluber's 47.1012 Behind him Espino, Erik Sabrowski and Hunter Gaddis carried the ball to Cade Smith, whose four-out save ran his month to a 1.00 earned-run average with 13 strikeouts in nine innings. Tampa Bay's consolations were small but genuine: Liam Hicks threw out two Cleveland runners, the first Rays catcher ever to cut down two in a postseason game.12

The visitors' grief is the bats. Three hits and 13 strikeouts on the afternoon; Junior Caminero 0-for-4 with four of them, his first postseason homer still unstruck; the top third of the order — Díaz, Jonathan Aranda, Caminero — a combined 1-for-12. "We have to make adjustments and play our baseball," Caminero said through the club's interpreter, and his manager Kevin Cash asked plainly for bigger at-bats.10 So Cleveland leads two games to one and stands two victories from its first World's Series since 2016 — the fourth time the franchise has held such a lead in a pennant round, having cashed the one in 1997 and let go those of 1998 and 2007 — while Tampa Bay trails at this station for the first time in its history; the scholars note the winner of a third game from a 1-1 tie has taken the series in roughly seven cases of ten.1012 The fourth game is appointed for eight o'clock tonight by the lake, weather permitting, and the Weather Desk sets out the particulars — and the contingencies — elsewhere in this number.2

News Around the League

THE LAUREL DESK: THE MOST VALUABLE MAN OF THE NATIONAL ROUND NEARLY QUIT THE GAME TWO WINTERS PAST — BAUERS, SIX RUNS DRIVEN IN AND A HIT IN EVERY GAME, IS THE FIRST BREWER EVER TO CARRY OFF THE HONOR, AND EITHER AMERICAN FINALIST IS A FORMER EMPLOYER

The hardware followed the story. Jake Bauers, whose twelve-pitch walk turned the second game and whose eleven-pitch homer turned the third — both sieges set out at length in these columns — was named the most valuable player of the National League's round on the field Thursday night, the first man in Milwaukee's history to take the series laurel. The affidavit: a hit in all four games, a team-leading six runs driven in — tied for the most in any postseason series the franchise has played — and in the clincher a two-run double and the bases-loaded walk that drew the game level.9

The man receives the honor at 31, in his seventh season, two winters removed from nearly leaving the game altogether before his wife talked him back onto the field. The regular season that followed ran to 26 home runs and 86 runs batted in, and October has compounded it. "I just let it all come to me," Bauers said. "I didn't chase it." His teammates were less restrained — "No one deserves it more," said Sal Frelick — and his manager chose the house style: "Jake played with a broken toe, he's had shin splints all year, and he's soft," offered Pat Murphy, entirely in jest.9 The footnote the deadball desks will savor: Bauers broke into the league with Tampa Bay in 2018 and spent two seasons in Cleveland's employ, so whichever club emerges from the American round, the World's Series will send the series' most valuable man against a former employer.9

THE WEATHER DESK: THE AMERICAN ROUND'S FOURTH GAME GOES TONIGHT AT EIGHT BY THE LAKE, IF THE SKY ALLOWS — MARTINEZ, WHO BLANKED CLEVELAND TWICE THIS SUMMER ACROSS THIRTEEN INNINGS, MEETS A HOME STAFF ASSEMBLED BY COMMITTEE, AND A WASHOUT WOULD REDRAW THE WEEK

The American League's fourth sitting is appointed for eight o'clock Eastern tonight at Progressive Field, Cleveland leading two games to one — but the sky holds a vote. Rain is in the Friday forecast, the same forecast that moved yesterday's game up to one o'clock in the afternoon, and both commands spent Thursday drawing contingencies. Should the evening prove unplayable, the clubs could pass Friday idle and play the fourth and fifth games Saturday and Sunday by the lake, spending the scheduled travel day, with a sixth game to follow at the Gulf without pause.132

If the game is played tonight, Tampa Bay sends Nick Martinez, a right-hander of career-high employment this season — 31 starts, a 15-6 record and a 3.10 earned-run average — who holds a peculiar mastery of the home side: two starts against Cleveland this summer, thirteen innings, not one run, including seven blank frames in a 1-0 verdict in this very yard in April. Drew Rasmussen stands slated for the fifth game and Freddy Peralta for the sixth.1312 Cleveland's answer is a committee: a bullpen evening in which Joey Cantillo is expected to carry a large share, Tanner Bibee and Slade Cecconi the bulk innings, and Shawn Armstrong — unscored upon in four October appearances — or Daniel Espino may be first out of the gate. A postponement would change the committee's complexion entirely, handing Foster Griffin the ball Saturday on regular rest. "Our guys stay ready," said Stephen Vogt, declining to be alarmed on either count.1312

THE ALMANAC DESK: THE WORLD'S SERIES OPENS FRIDAY NEXT AT MILWAUKEE — HOME GROUND EARNED BY A HUNDRED AND THREE VICTORIES, THE FIRST TWO GAMES AND ANY SIXTH AND SEVENTH BY THE LAKESIDE BREWERY, AND THE AMERICAN CHAMPION TO BE KNOWN BY THEN

The almanac may now be printed in ink. The 122nd World's Series opens Friday, October 23, at American Family Field in Milwaukee, with the second game there Saturday the 24th; the third, fourth and fifth games go Monday the 26th through Wednesday the 28th at the American champion's grounds; and a sixth and seventh, should the argument require them, return to Milwaukee on Friday the 30th and Saturday the 31st.142

The home ground is held on merit, not on league custom: the Brewers' 103-59 was the best record in the majors, a franchise mark, and it outranks whatever the American round produces — Tampa Bay having won 98 and Cleveland fewer still. Every game goes out over the FOX wire. Start times await the league's pleasure, and the opponent awaits tonight's weather; both will be entered in this ledger the morning after they are known.14

THE FAREWELL DESK: ROJAS, AGED SEVEN-AND-THIRTY, TELLS HIS TEAMMATES 'THIS IS IT' — THIRTEEN SEASONS, TWO TITLES, A NO-HITTER PRESERVED WITH THE BACKHAND AND A SEVENTH-GAME HOMER IN THE NINTH, AND NOW A DESK IN THE DODGERS' SCHOOLHOUSE

The last game of the National League's season was also the last of a distinguished career. Miguel Rojas, 37 years old, told his Los Angeles teammates after Thursday's defeat that he had played his final game as an active man: "This is it, guys. This is it." The ledger he closes runs thirteen major-league seasons and 21 years in professional baseball — a 2014 debut with these same Dodgers, remembered for the backhand stop at third base that helped preserve Clayton Kershaw's June no-hitter; eight seasons as Miami's everyday shortstop and captain; and a return to Los Angeles in 2023 for four seasons, 446 games and a .260 average.15

The crowning entries came late, as they sometimes do for the glove men: World's Series titles in 2024 and 2025, and in the seventh game of last autumn's Series against Toronto, a game-tying home run in the ninth inning — a swing that will outlive every fielding chart ever drawn of him. He does not go far: Rojas moves into a player-development post with the organization, the exact title still being lettered. "He built a legacy that we'll be talking about for a long time," said Freddie Freeman; Mookie Betts called him simply "our leader." The Herald tips its cap to a workman of the old school and wishes him a long second career teaching the backhand.15

With this number the Herald's ledger turns one hundred — a hundred mornings of scores set down and deeds sung since this desk first took up its pen, and the chronicle is pleased to mark the occasion with a pennant in it. The forward ledger now reads: the American round's fourth game tonight at eight by the lake, weather permitting, a fifth Saturday at the same address, and a sixth Monday at the Gulf should the argument run on; the National League's business is concluded until Friday next, the 23rd, when the World's Series opens at Milwaukee.213 One league's season ended last night in a glove in left-center; the other's hangs tonight on a rain cloud over Lake Erie. The game, as ever, keeps its own calendar and lets the rest of us guess. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE FIRST PITCH OF THE EVENING LEAVES THE YARD AND THE ELEVENTH OF A SINGLE SIEGE DECIDES IT — CHOURIO AMBUSHES SNELL BEFORE THE FIFTY THOUSAND HAVE SETTLED, BAUERS OUTLASTS HIM FOR A GO-AHEAD CLOUT, MITCHELL FOLLOWS HIM OVER THE BARRIER, AND MILWAUKEE STANDS ONE VICTORY FROM ITS FIRST WORLD'S SERIES IN FOUR-AND-FORTY YEARS: BREWERS 6, DODGERS 2
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 99 · Thursday, the Fifteenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE FIRST PITCH OF THE EVENING LEAVES THE YARD AND THE ELEVENTH OF A SINGLE SIEGE DECIDES IT — CHOURIO AMBUSHES SNELL BEFORE THE FIFTY THOUSAND HAVE SETTLED, BAUERS OUTLASTS HIM FOR A GO-AHEAD CLOUT, MITCHELL FOLLOWS HIM OVER THE BARRIER, AND MILWAUKEE STANDS ONE VICTORY FROM ITS FIRST WORLD'S SERIES IN FOUR-AND-FORTY YEARS: BREWERS 6, DODGERS 2

Jackson Chourio strikes Blake Snell's very first offering into the right-center seats — one year to the day after he opened a postseason game the same way — and after Will Smith's bases-loaded double briefly restores the champions and their crowd, Jake Bauers fouls off everything Snell has left and turns the eleventh pitch of the battle into a two-run homer, Garrett Mitchell makes it back-to-back, and the Dodgers stand three games down in a hole only one club in history has ever climbed out of

Dodger Stadium got its voice back in the sixth inning Wednesday night, and kept it for less than an inning. Will Smith, mired all month, had just lined a bases-loaded double off the top of the left-center wall for the lead, and the 50,708 were making the old championship noise — two titles running will teach a crowd the words. Then Jake Bauers stepped in against Blake Snell in the seventh and declined, pitch after pitch after pitch, to be put away, and when the eleventh offering caught too much of the plate he deposited it in the right-field pavilion, 412 feet off, for two runs and the lead.34 The yard went so quiet that the visitors' dugout could be heard celebrating in the upper deck. Garrett Mitchell struck the next homer himself, back-to-back, and Milwaukee had turned a 2-1 deficit into a 6-2 verdict and a three-games-to-none grip on the National League's pennant round.3

The evening had announced its character on its very first pitch. Jackson Chourio, 22 years old, met Snell's opening fastball — 97.6 miles the hour, center-cut — and drove it the opposite way into the right-center seats before some of the principals had found their places; the Milwaukee owner was still scrambling to his seat, and Bauers was still pulling on his batting gloves.6 The records went scrambling with him: only six men have opened a postseason game with a first-pitch home run since such things were first counted in 1988, and Chourio has now done it twice — one year to the day since he did it in this same round against this same club — a distinction he shares with George Springer alone. The blow was his sixth postseason homer, the most any Brewer has ever accumulated, and Snell became the only pitcher twice victimized by the leadoff ambush.6 The young man played the rest of his evening in company: a praying mantis took up residence on his shoulder in the third, just as he settled under a Freddie Freeman fly ball half-lost in the low sun, and could not be persuaded off him. The catch was made, insect and all.7

Between the first blow and the last ran a proper pitchers' evening. Snell, who had not allowed a home run in ten starts this year, gathered himself after Chourio's clout and at one stretch retired fourteen men in succession, nine strikeouts among his evening's work.54 Robert Gasser — the man this paper introduced yesterday as the season's quietest success — answered with five scoreless innings of his own, three hits, on 72 pitches. The sixth undid the visitors' arithmetic for a moment: Abner Uribe arrived from the bullpen without his compass, walked three Dodgers, and Smith's double cashed two of them — the heaviest damage Milwaukee's relief corps has absorbed all month, with a blown save entered against Uribe's account. DL Hall walked in, stranded Shohei Ohtani ninety feet from home, and the damage stopped at two.35

Then came the seventh, and the at-bat that may yet stand as the series' epitaph. Andrew Vaughn's seven-pitch walk ended Snell's run of fourteen straight; Christian Yelich went in to run for him; and Bauers — who turned the second game Monday with a twelve-pitch walk against Yoshinobu Yamamoto — began fouling off everything with a star on it. A called strike, two balls, a foul tip; two-strike fouls off the slider and the curve; ball three; then fouls off the four-seamer, the changeup, the slider again. The eleventh pitch was a fastball meant for the edge that arrived at the middle, and Bauers did not miss it. He is the second man in postseason history with plate appearances of eleven pitches or more in consecutive games — the Cubs' Aramis Ramirez, in 2003, is the other — and his homer was just the sixth ever struck on the eleventh pitch or later of a postseason at-bat.4 The beaten pitcher, once his teammate in the Tampa Bay chain, paid him the evening's handsomest tribute: "I've seen all the ups and downs he's been through, and it's been a lot of downs. For him to go through this right now, he's earned it. Hat's off to him. What an at-bat. I threw everything I had."4 This is, after all, a man Milwaukee itself released two Novembers ago, a journeyman of five organizations who once mused about quitting the game for Costa Rica. "I was looking for a fastball, and I didn't want to miss it," Bauers said. "I said I'll adjust to anything else, but if you get a heater, don't miss it."4

Mitchell's four-bagger made the pair the third set of back-to-back postseason homers in Milwaukee's annals and chased Snell; a wild pitch cashed Brice Turang in the eighth and Joey Ortiz singled home Cooper Pratt in the ninth, and the accounting was complete. The visitors have now answered, immediately and in kind, every one of the four innings in which Los Angeles has scored in this series — their fifth comeback victory in seven October games, a figure matched this early only by the 1996 Yankees and 1980 Phillies, both of whom finished their autumns with parades.3 The arithmetic ahead is the kind this paper prints with a steady hand: of the 42 clubs ever down three games to none in a best-of-seven, 32 were swept, two forced a seventh game, and exactly one — the 2004 Red Sox, on whose roster stood a reserve outfielder named Dave Roberts — recovered the series. "It's certainly possible," says the same Roberts, now managing the club that must do it. "I've lived it."5 His batsmen, 3-for-32 with runners in scoring position this postseason outside Smith's double, are rather further from the precedent than he is. Kyle Tucker states the assignment plainly: "This team's won four games before. That's what we're going to have to do."3 The fourth game goes this very evening at eight o'clock Eastern at Dodger Stadium, and the Elimination Desk takes up its particulars elsewhere in this number.10

News Around the League

THE ELIMINATION DESK: TONIGHT AT EIGHT THE CHAMPIONS BAT FOR THEIR LIVES BEHIND GLASNOW, UNDEFEATED COMPANY IN THIS OCTOBER'S SEVEN ERRANDS — MILWAUKEE, ASKED FOR ITS STARTER, PROMISES ONLY THAT 'THERE WILL BE PITCHING'

The National League's fourth sitting goes tonight at eight o'clock Eastern at Dodger Stadium — moved up an hour from nine by the league's Wednesday decree — with the sweep standing one game off and the champions' three-peat standing on its last legal appeal.810

Los Angeles sends its best remaining argument. Los Angeles has yet to lose a postseason game in which Tyler Glasnow has pitched this month — seven appearances, a 1.73 earned-run average across 26 innings — and the man carries a 3.60 figure in three career elimination games, all served in Tampa Bay's employ. His last outing wobbled, five walks against Atlanta in the Division round, but surrendered a single run in 4 2/3 innings.10 Behind him the bullpen reports in nearly full strength, though the first two games' starters do not: Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto are held back for a fifth and sixth game that will exist only if tonight is won.510

Milwaukee, meanwhile, conducted the week's briefest press conference. "Pitching tomorrow?" a reporter asked Pat Murphy, hoping for a name. "Yeah," the manager replied, "there will be pitching."10 The candidates for what amounts to a bullpen evening are plentiful and rested: the left-handers Kyle Harrison and Shane Drohan and the right-hander Chad Patrick have yet to throw a pitch in seven postseason games, and Dustin May — a former Dodger with a 2020 ring from this very ballpark — threw an inning in the second game. The staff they would front carries a 1.74 earned-run average this postseason, the lowest of the twelve clubs that entered.10 The champions have twice lately climbed from the brink — down two games to one against San Diego in 2024, down three games to two in last year's World's Series — but they have never needed four victories in a row with winter at the door. "We've never been in this big of a hole," says Kiké Hernández, "but we've had our backs against the wall plenty of times before, and we've come out of it."5

THE LAKEFRONT DESK: RAIN MOVES THE AMERICAN QUESTION TO ONE O'CLOCK IN THE AFTERNOON — WILLIAMS, NOW OFFICIAL, TAKES THE BALL FOR THE FOREST CITY NINE AGAINST JAX, WHO MAKES THE FIRST OCTOBER START OF HIS LIFE IN A YARD HE KNOWS BY HEART

The American League's pennant round resumes today at Progressive Field at one o'clock in the afternoon, Eastern — the league having moved the game up five full hours from its evening appointment on account of rain forecast over Cleveland tonight. October baseball by daylight, by the lake, with the round tied at a game apiece: the deadball desks could ask no better page.89

The pitching is now official on both sides. Gavin Williams, whom this paper reckoned yesterday the likely man, was formally named Wednesday afternoon — on regular rest at last, after a Division round in which he made two starts and an emergency relief errand, recorded the final three outs of the fourth game, and came back on one day's rest to strike out twelve in the fifth, tying the franchise's postseason record. His October ledger stands at a 1.54 earned-run average with 24 strikeouts in 11 2/3 innings, and today's assignment lines him up, should the series run its full length, to start a seventh game Tuesday on regular rest.9 Opposite him, Griffin Jax makes the first postseason start of his career — a starter most of this season, lately a reliever by October necessity, with a 0.90 earned-run average over his last five appearances; since a rough return from elbow discomfort in early September, he has permitted two runs in 20 innings with 19 strikeouts across his last four regular-season starts and a Division-round relief errand. The venue holds no mysteries for him: most of his career was spent in Minnesota's employ, and his 13 relief appearances in this very yard produced a 2.19 earned-run average. The man is presumably also acquainted with the weather.9

The crowd that sang Cleveland back from two defeats down against Chicago now gets three straight home dates with the round level — and the statisticians' note from yesterday's number still stands: the winner of a third game in a series tied at one has gone on to take the series in roughly seven cases of ten. Patrick Bailey, swinging a hot October bat, catches his customary partner; Tampa Bay's lone question is whether Jonny DeLuca or Cedric Mullins patrols center.9

THE MANAGERIAL DESK: THE COURTSHIP THIS PAPER REPORTED YESTERDAY LOSES ITS CHAPERONE — HOUSTON LETS ESPADA'S PAPERS LAPSE A DAY AFTER LENDING HIM TO SEATTLE'S PARLOR, AND PHILADELPHIA, TWICE REFUSED BY CORA, GIVES MATTINGLY, AGED FIVE-AND-SIXTY, TWO YEARS ON MERIT

The managerial market produced two settlements Wednesday, and the first reads as a sequel to yesterday's number. Joe Espada, whose permission to interview for Seattle's vacancy this paper reported only yesterday, will not be back in Houston at all: the Astros announced they will not renew his contract when it expires at the month's end. The owner Jim Crane supplied the customary warm send-off — "We are thankful for Joe's hard work, his passion for the game, and for his commitment to the Houston Astros" — and the club parted besides with five of its coaches, leaving it in search of a manager and a general manager at once, Dana Brown having been dismissed in August.12 The record Espada carries to market: 256 wins against 229 across three seasons, division flags in 2024 and 2026 — the latter at 81-81, the first club in the game's history to reach the postseason without a winning record — and a two-game sweep at the White Sox's hands for an exit. The courtship across the division may now proceed without asking anyone's leave.12

In Philadelphia, meantime, the interim tag came off. Don Mattingly, 65 years old, signed a two-year engagement as the Phillies' manager, the position he has held in fact since Rob Thomson's dismissal 28 games into the season. His case argued itself: 79 wins against 55 thereafter, a Wild Card berth clinched with a victory in the season's final game, and an exit in the deciding third game of the Wild Card round against Atlanta. The appointment carries its footnotes — the man is the father of the club's general manager Preston Mattingly, and the executive Dave Dombrowski was twice rebuffed in his pursuit of Alex Cora before settling, both times, on the man already in the chair.13 The Herald observes that 23 consecutive seasons of managing and coaching, laid atop a playing career of the first order, make "settling" a curious word for it.

THE AWARDS DESK: RAWLINGS NAMES THREE MEN TO EVERY POST FOR THE GOLDEN GLOVES, VERDICTS SEALED UNTIL THE FIRST OF NOVEMBER — AND TWO OF THE NOMINATED WILL BE AT WORK THIS VERY AFTERNOON BY THE LAKE

The leather trade published its short lists Wednesday: the Gold Glove finalists for 2026, three men to a position in each league, the utility post included, with the winners to be announced on the first of November. The electorate, for the record, is the league's 30 managers and up to six coaches per club, barred from voting for their own men and counting for three-quarters of the verdict, the remaining quarter supplied by the Society for American Baseball Research's defensive index.11 The Blue Jays and Cubs lead the nominations with five men apiece; the Braves, Diamondbacks, Rangers and Royals count four each.11

Two of the nominated have more immediate engagements. Tanner Bibee, a finalist among American League pitchers, and Taylor Walls, a finalist at shortstop, are presently employed on opposite sides of the pennant round that resumes at one o'clock today at Progressive Field — Bibee for Cleveland, Walls for Tampa Bay — and may be excused for leaving the campaigning to their rivals.11 The Herald reports nominations as nominations, per its standing rule: the hardware changes hands when the ballots are counted, and not an edition sooner.

Today the calendar grants both arguments at once, and at civilized intervals: the American question at one o'clock in the afternoon by the lake, where the rain rewrote the timetable, and the National at eight in Los Angeles, where Milwaukee may finish what it started and the champions must win tonight and then three more times besides. Friday holds the American round's fourth game at Cleveland, and a fifth National sitting — should tonight's defendants earn it.2 An afternoon playoff game is the oldest luxury the sport affords: it was how all of October sounded before the lights went up, and a reader with a flexible luncheon arrangement is advised to take full advantage. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
