entry.title: THE SECRET IS ANNOUNCED OVER THE LOUD-SPEAKER AND KEPT ANYWAY — ONE-AND-SEVENTY FASTBALLS FROM 'FASTBALL FREDDY,' THE SWIFTEST OF HIS NINE-YEAR LIFE; A GROUND BALL FINDS THE ONE CRACK IN THE LEAGUE'S SUREST THIRD BASEMAN; AND THE THROWBACK-CLAD RAYS SQUARE THE PENNANT ROUND: RAYS 3, GUARDIANS 1
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 98 · Wednesday, the Fourteenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE SECRET IS ANNOUNCED OVER THE LOUD-SPEAKER AND KEPT ANYWAY — ONE-AND-SEVENTY FASTBALLS FROM 'FASTBALL FREDDY,' THE SWIFTEST OF HIS NINE-YEAR LIFE; A GROUND BALL FINDS THE ONE CRACK IN THE LEAGUE'S SUREST THIRD BASEMAN; AND THE THROWBACK-CLAD RAYS SQUARE THE PENNANT ROUND: RAYS 3, GUARDIANS 1

Kevin Cash grumbles that even the public-address man was advertising 'Fastball Freddy' before the first pitch — then Peralta throws 71 four-seamers among his 99 pitches regardless, 29 of them at 97 miles the hour or better and one at 99.4, the hardest of his career, across six scoreless innings in the longest postseason outing of his life; Tampa Bay's three runs, every one unearned, are manufactured from a walk, two infield choppers, an alert dash to an unguarded base and a ball that skips through José Ramírez's legs; and Parker Messick's boyhood-ballpark homecoming ends in a tough-luck defeat as the series packs for Cleveland tied at a game apiece

The evening's one secret was given away before the first pitch, and it kept perfectly well anyway. "The announcers before the game and even our PA were calling him 'Fastball Freddy,'" Kevin Cash grumbled afterward, half in jest. "That told everybody what was coming."4 What came, Tuesday night at Tropicana Field, was 71 four-seam fastballs among Freddy Peralta's 99 pitches — a reliance he had not permitted himself in any start since June of 2019 — and the forewarned Guardians went 3-for-17 against the pitch and never once scratched him.4 The figures read like an affidavit: 29 offerings at 97 miles the hour or better from a man whose season average was 94.3; a 99.4 to Jo Adell in the fifth, the hardest pitch of his nine-year career; 51 of the 71 heaters spotted at the top third of the strike zone or above it.43 "It's already an elite fastball, but he was placing it at the top for strikes," said Steven Kwan. "And then it felt like when he wanted to, he just put it a ball above. When he's doing that, it's pretty hard to lay off."4 Six scoreless innings — the longest postseason errand of Peralta's life — on four singles, two walks and a hit batsman, closed with a nine-pitch siege of Petey Halpin that ended in a changeup, a strikeout, a scream off the mound and the dome chanting "Freddy! Freddy!" at the Trade Deadline acquisition. His last eight starts, summer and October together, have now each allowed five hits or fewer and no more than one run, with a Tampa Bay victory to show for every one — the longest such run by any traditional starter since 1900.4

The three runs behind him were all unearned and all of a piece — "a very Rays inning," their own manager certified.6 Junior Caminero opened the fourth with a walk; Victor Mesa Jr.'s double-play bouncer was undone on review, the relay having pulled Nathaniel Lowe's foot from the bag; and after a strikeout, Chandler Simpson — making his first start since the second game of the Division round — chopped a ball five feet in front of the plate and outran the clean play. Mesa, observing that third base stood unguarded where Ramírez had drifted toward short, simply never stopped running.6 Then Ben Williamson beat a 2-1 changeup into the ground toward the surest glove in the league, and the ball struck the lip where the dirt meets the artificial turf, hopped off the top of Ramírez's mitt and passed between his legs into left field as Mesa trotted home.65 Liam Hicks, dropped to eighth in the order against the left hand, lined the next man's first pitch — a slider left up — to right-center for two more. One ball out of the infield in the whole rally, and the game decided by it. "They've done that all year," said Stephen Vogt. "When they smell blood, they take it and run."3

Cleveland's grief wants a careful accounting, for the club otherwise played a clean, hard game. Ramírez makes the play in question as near to always as the language allows; this once the bounce defeated him. "Nobody's perfect, but I still feel bad," the third baseman said through the club's interpreter. "The ball bounced right on the edge between the dirt and the turf. That's what made it more difficult for me."5 Kwan, who was himself victimized by the surface in the opener, offered the visiting fielder's lament: "It's kind of inconsistent whether it's going to hop or skip. When you don't play on it every day, you're just not calibrated to it."5 The offense supplied its own share, going 1-for-6 with runners in scoring position and leaving nine men aboard; the lone reply was Chase DeLauter's double to right in the seventh, cashing Patrick Bailey's walk.5 And Messick — whose homecoming to the ballpark of his boyhood this paper set out at length yesterday morning — deserved a kinder ledger than the one he signed: five innings, six hits, two walks, three runs and not one of them earned, a tough-luck defeat in the house he once watched from the cheap seats.5

The victors, it should be recorded, played the evening in fancy dress. Down a game, the Rays swapped into their Devil Rays throwbacks around ten o'clock that morning on a suggestion from the club's chief executive Ken Babby — a costume in which they had gone 12-3 during the regular season — and the swagger arrived with the wardrobe.7 Caminero leapt to spear Kwan's fifth-inning liner and administered a finger wag after the fashion of Dikembe Mutombo; by the seventh the two were conferring amiably at third base about it. "He told me, 'Hey, if I hit it a little bit harder, the ball's past you,'" Caminero reported. "And I said, 'Yeah, try to hit it harder and I won't catch it.'"7 So the 32,125 went home in two hours and forty-two minutes, and the round removes to the lakefront tied at one — no small adjustment of the odds, the home-field club having historically taken such a series 55 times in 102, and 24 of 40 in the pennant rounds. The third game goes Thursday evening at six o'clock Eastern at Progressive Field, and the Herald surveys that sitting elsewhere in this number.32

News Around the League

THE LINEUP DESK: THE QUESTION OF RESTING OHTANI IS ANSWERED BY THE MAN HIMSELF — 'ADAMANT' HE CAN HELP, THE GAME'S GREATEST INSTRUMENT TAKES HIS PLACE IN TONIGHT'S ORDER, MECHANICS, SYMPTOMS AND ALL

The conversation this paper reported yesterday has been held, and the player won it. Shohei Ohtani will bat for Los Angeles in tonight's third game, Dave Roberts announced Tuesday at Dodger Stadium, the club having weighed resting him and found the man immovable. "He was very convicted that he is onto something mechanically," the manager said. "He was adamant that he can help us. He's well enough to help us win a baseball game. So that's all I needed to hear."8 Roberts likened the sitting-down he did not order to the one he once gave Freddie Freeman, whose sprained ankle cost him three games of the 2024 postseason before five World Series appearances that entered legend.8

The figures that prompted the question have not improved for being aired. Ohtani stands at .197 with a .629 on-base-plus-slugging over his last 35 games, has not homered since August 18 — a drought of 110 plate appearances, the longest of his career — and is 3-for-20 this October without an extra-base hit, dropped from second in the order to cleanup. Speaking to the press for the first time since the eve of the Division round, he declined the alibi of the right biceps and left knee that have troubled him since June: "The symptoms shouldn't be the reason why I can't hit," he said through his interpreter.8 The remedies have been uncharacteristic — on-field batting practice four days running, from a man who takes it in public a handful of times a year, and even a show of bunt against a left-handed reliever on Monday.8 The opposition declines to read the ledger literally. "We remember vividly at this time last year that he maybe had the best baseball game ever played the day he pitched against us," said Milwaukee's Pat Murphy. "You can't forget that, his capabilities, whatever."8 On that much, every scorer in the press box agrees.

THE PRECIPICE DESK: TONIGHT AT EIGHT THE TWICE-CROWNED CHAMPIONS MAKE THEIR STAND AT HOME, TWO GAMES IN ARREARS — SNELL, WHO FACED THE MINIMUM THROUGH EIGHT AGAINST THESE SAME BREWERS A YEAR AGO, DRAWS THE ASSIGNMENT AGAINST GASSER, A MAN WHO BEGAN THIS SEASON IN NASHVILLE

The National League's argument resumes tonight at eight o'clock Eastern at Dodger Stadium, and the arithmetic of the precipice is plainly printed: clubs down two games to none in a best-of-seven have recovered the series 16 times in 95 trials, and of the 42 that ever fell behind three games to none, 32 were swept and exactly one — Roberts' own 2004 Red Sox, as the manager hardly needs reminding — climbed all the way out.9 "You want to get that first one," Roberts allows.9

His chosen instrument is the left hand with the best claim on Milwaukee's respect. Blake Snell, limited to nine starts this season by shoulder trouble and surgery on the elbow, was "too fine" by his manager's reckoning in his lone October outing, walking five men in an abbreviated Division-round start; but his five starts at Dodger Stadium this year show a 2.19 earned-run average, and his last acquaintance with these Brewers — in this very round, a year ago — ran eight scoreless innings in which he struck out ten and faced the minimum.910 "0-2, 2-0, it wouldn't matter," Snell said. "I know what I need to do to win and dominate." His teammate Teoscar Hernández counts the remaining cards without blinking: "We've got Snell, we've got Glasnow, and then we've got Tarik again... I think we're going to be OK."10

Milwaukee's answer is the season's quietest success story: Robert Gasser, who opened the year at Triple-A Nashville and enters a pennant-round start on a run of 2-0 with a 1.73 earned-run average over his last seven appearances — a rise that began in late August when a comebacker felled Dustin May on the game's first pitch and Gasser walked out of the bullpen into a rotation he has not left since.9 With Milwaukee's fourth-game starter yet unnamed, every inning the sweeper-artist supplies tonight is worth two. The home crowd, the probabilities and the champions' pride all report for duty at the same hour; the Herald will believe the obituaries when it sees the body.9

THE LAKEFRONT DESK: THE AMERICAN ROUND, NOW A BEST-OF-FIVE WITH THREE GAMES BY THE LAKE, RECONVENES THURSDAY AT SIX — JAX IS NAMED FOR TAMPA BAY, WILLIAMS STANDS LIKELY FOR CLEVELAND, AND THE LOUDEST YARD OF THE AUTUMN AWAITS THEM BOTH

The American League's pennant round rests today and reconvenes Thursday at six o'clock Eastern at Progressive Field, reduced by the split at the dome to a best-of-five in which Cleveland holds the next three home dates.112 The statisticians commend the appointment: in best-of-seven series knotted at one, the third game's winner has gone on to take the series 71 times in 102.5

Tampa Bay has named its man — Griffin Jax, a starter for most of the season, who carries a 0.90 earned-run average over his last five appearances and spent only 32 pitches in his lone Division-round errand, two tidy innings against the Yankees.11 Cleveland has named nobody, Vogt preferring to see how his staff emerges from the first two games, but the ball figures to belong to Gavin Williams on regular rest — the same Williams whose Division round ran to a 1.54 earned-run average with 24 strikeouts in 11 2/3 innings, closing one elimination game and starting the next.11

The venue is reckoned a combatant in its own right. The lakefront crowd that sang its club back from two games dead against Chicago now receives a series tied, and even the enemy tips his cap in advance. "That's as good an atmosphere as you're going to see," said Kevin Cash. "They've got a great fan base that's going to be behind their team."11 The marquee names, meanwhile, owe the round a signature: Ramírez's series so far holds one solid game and one costly error, and Caminero still awaits the first postseason home run of his career. One of the two clubs will put the sport's longest waits another game behind it Thursday — Cleveland's drought of 77 seasons against a Tampa Bay franchise that has never once, in 28 years, carried the flag home.11

THE MANAGERIAL DESK: SEATTLE ASKS LEAVE TO COURT THE MAN WHO KEPT HOUSTON'S MACHINE RUNNING — ESPADA, HIS CONTRACT EXPIRING WITH THE MONTH, WILL HEAR THE MARINERS OUT

Word from the executive corridors: Joe Espada, these past three seasons the manager of the Astros and for six before that their bench coach, will interview for Seattle's vacant managership, the Mariners having sought and received Houston's permission by the account of the wire's sources. Neither club confirms the courtship; the man's contract expires at the month's end, which rather confirms it for them.12

The résumé travels well. Espada's nine Houston years took in the 2022 championship, two further pennants and seven division titles, and his own three seasons at the helm ran 256-229 with the West's flag in 2024 and again this summer — though this summer's edition won it at 81-81 and was swept from the Wild Card round by the White Sox, a decline that had already cost the general manager Dana Brown his post in August.12 Espada, for his part, has said plainly he would like to continue in Houston.

Seattle's specification reads like a reply to its own history: the president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto — whose two previous selections, Scott Servais and the departed Dan Wilson, had never managed a game at any level — now declares prior big-league experience "preferred" and the need to be for "fresh thought."12 A man with three division titles in three years, suddenly at liberty across the division, answers the advertisement almost suspiciously well. The Herald files the courtship under October's quieter competitions and will report the banns if they are published.12

A single game stands on tonight's card, and it may be the month's heaviest: the National League's third sitting, at eight o'clock Eastern at Dodger Stadium, where the champions of the last two World's Series stand twice beaten, with Snell on the hill and Ohtani batting on his own insistence. Thursday the calendar doubles again — Tampa Bay at Cleveland at six o'clock, Milwaukee at Los Angeles at nine.2 The week's two evenings at the dome have supplied a matched pair of lessons: Monday the form sheet burned, and Tuesday it was lovingly restored, the best fastball of a man's life and a single error punished to the last unearned run. The game gives and takes away with the same hand, and October keeps every receipt. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE ONE-AND-NINETIETH PITCH IS THE ACE'S LAST, AND IT COMES DOWN FOUR HUNDRED AND THIRTY-SIX FEET AWAY — DeLAUTER AND BAILEY UNDO RASMUSSEN BY INSTALLMENTS, LOWE UNTIES THE KNOT, AND THE LAKE ERIE MEN, FOUR TIMES VICTORIOUS RUNNING, CARRY THE OPENER OUT OF THE ENEMY'S DOME: GUARDIANS 7, RAYS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 97 · Tuesday, the Thirteenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 2 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE ONE-AND-NINETIETH PITCH IS THE ACE'S LAST, AND IT COMES DOWN FOUR HUNDRED AND THIRTY-SIX FEET AWAY — DeLAUTER AND BAILEY UNDO RASMUSSEN BY INSTALLMENTS, LOWE UNTIES THE KNOT, AND THE LAKE ERIE MEN, FOUR TIMES VICTORIOUS RUNNING, CARRY THE OPENER OUT OF THE ENEMY'S DOME: GUARDIANS 7, RAYS 3

Down 2-0 by the first inning to a Tampa Bay club that had not lost a game since the regular season's final Sunday, Cleveland waits out Drew Rasmussen — whose previous 13 starts had every one of them ended in a Rays victory — and then dismantles the evening piece by piece: Chase DeLauter's opposite-field homer in the sixth, Patrick Bailey's 436-foot reply on the ace's 91st and final pitch to open the seventh, Nathaniel Lowe's two-run single in the eighth, and a three-run ninth manufactured largely by José Ramírez's legs, while Foster Griffin and five relievers hold the American League's top seed to one run across the final eight innings

For five innings beneath the dome at St. Petersburg on Monday night, the pennant round's American opener obeyed the form sheet to the letter. The Rays, 98 games victorious this summer and unbeaten since the 27th of September, scored twice before Cleveland had recorded three outs — Junior Caminero and Jonny DeLuca singling home the runs in the first — and Drew Rasmussen, rested to the point of luxury, carried the 2-0 advantage through six innings on 90 pitches, pitching as a man whose previous 13 starts had every one concluded in a Tampa Bay win.34 The house brand was all in evidence: the airtight glovework, the opportune single, the strangling of the opposing offense. The visitors from the lake, fresh from three straight elimination wins in the Chicago round, were being quietly shown the arithmetic by a club that had been resting on its sweep of the Yankees.4

Then Chase DeLauter leaned on a pitch and drove it the opposite way, over the left-field barrier, and the form sheet began to smolder. That was the sixth inning and made it 2-1; in the seventh, Tampa Bay elected to send Rasmussen out once more, and Patrick Bailey met the ace's 91st pitch — his first of the inning, and his last of the night — and deposited it 436 feet to right-center, the longest blow of the catcher's major-league life, for the tie.3 "We got punched early," said the Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt. "Our pitching staff, credit to them for stopping it and keeping us in the game as long as they did. The offense came alive... Hitting a couple balls out of the yard made it a new game."3

The new game belonged to the visitors. In the eighth, José Ramírez and DeLauter singled their way aboard against the reliever Wells, and Nathaniel Lowe lined a two-run single to center off Ian Seymour — both runs entered against Wells's account, and the defeat with them — to put Cleveland ahead 4-2 to a roar from the traveling contingent.4 Cedric Mullins answered with a solo shot off Erik Sabrowski in the bottom half, and then the ninth dissolved into the particular chaos that follows José Ramírez around October. A tag play, overturned on Cleveland's challenge, let Angel Martínez score on Ramírez's single; moments later Ramírez widened his lead off second until the pitcher Kevin Kelly could look at nothing else, broke with the delivery, and drew Caminero sprinting to third to cover — whereupon Jo Adell grounded a double through the ground the third baseman had just vacated, and two more runs crossed.4 "He's 'Hosey,'" said Vogt. "He just has a knack for finding his way on base. When he does, he makes things happen."4

The final accounting: 14 Cleveland hits, tied for the fourth-most the franchise has ever recorded in a nine-inning postseason game, and seven runs in the last four innings against a pitching apparatus that surrenders nothing by reputation.4 Behind Foster Griffin's four innings of two-run work came Daniel Espino, Joey Cantillo, Hunter Gaddis — the win credited to his name — Sabrowski and Cade Smith, an inning apiece.3 The victory is Cleveland's fourth without interruption, tied for the second-longest October streak in the franchise's annals behind the six that opened the 2016 tournament, and the club has scored 30 runs in the five games since it stood two defeats from winter.4 "There were some situations where this group definitely could have folded," said Lowe, reaching back to the Chicago series for his evidence, "but we didn't."3

So the round's first lead belongs to the lower seed, with the third, fourth and fifth games all waiting at Cleveland — no small matter between two clubs hauling the game's heaviest waits, the Guardians without a title since 1948 and the Rays without one in their 28 years of existence.5 Tampa Bay, for its part, declines the fainting couch. "We know exactly who we are," said Caminero. "We won 98 games for a reason. We won the division for a reason."3 The second game goes this very evening at eight o'clock Eastern at the dome, Parker Messick against Freddy Peralta, and the Herald takes up that pairing — a homecoming on one side, a resurrection on the other — elsewhere in this number.2

The Postseason Card

THRICE THE ANGELENOS NOSE AHEAD, AND THRICE THE ANSWER ARRIVES BEFORE THE INNING CAN CLOSE — WILD BILL STRIKES THREE BLOWS OF RECORD, BAUERS STANDS A TWELVE-PITCH SIEGE OF SEVEN MINUTES, AND THE CREAM CITY NINE GO TWO GAMES UP: BREWERS 7, DODGERS 4

Yamamoto, the reigning World Series Most Valuable Player, is run off after eight outs — the shortest postseason start of his life — by a third inning he cannot escape; William Contreras ties the game twice and wins it once, the fourth man in postseason history with three tying or go-ahead hits in a single game and the first since 1997; and four Milwaukee relievers retire all 15 men they face, the most wholly perfect bullpen innings any October game has ever recorded, as the series packs for Los Angeles with the titleholders in arrears

The second game of the National League round, before 42,516 at American Family Field on Monday, resolved into a call-and-answer the visitors could not win. Three times in the first six innings Los Angeles took a lead — Mookie Betts scoring on Teoscar Hernández's sacrifice fly in the first, Tommy Edman crossing on a thrown-away pickoff in the third, Kyle Tucker and Edman scoring in the fifth on a bunt heaved wide and Freddie Freeman's sacrifice fly — and three times Milwaukee drew level or better before the same inning closed.6 The visitors' four runs required only three hits, the home side's starter Logan Henderson having donated two throwing errors to the cause; the rest of their evening required rather more, and they did not have it. "They're playing really well over there," allowed Max Muncy afterward. "They're a very good team."6

The hinge of the night ran twelve pitches and seven minutes. With two aboard and two out in the third, Jake Bauers settled into a siege of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, fouling off six two-strike offerings from five different pitch types before the 12th pitch, a curveball, bounced for ball four — the longest plate appearance of Bauers' career, the longest anyone has forced upon Yamamoto in his American employ, and only the 12th postseason walk of a dozen pitches or more since such things were first counted in 1988.8 "It just got to a certain point where it was straight compete mode," said Bauers. "A little bit like a blackout." Two pitches later Christian Yelich lined Yamamoto's 75th and last offering into center for two runs, and the reigning World Series Most Valuable Player, who threw a complete game at this club in this round a year ago, was gone after eight outs, the briefest postseason start of his life. "He just didn't have it tonight," said Dave Roberts. "Which is very rare." His Milwaukee counterpart Pat Murphy called the walk "a turning point, I really do."86

And still the game required winning, which is where William Contreras conducted his clinic. The catcher dug a tying single out of his shoetops in the first; he tied it again in the fifth with a drive measured at 436 feet to straightaway center off Kris Bubic; and when the Dodgers put Brice Turang aboard on purpose in the sixth to face him, he lashed the go-ahead single to left and flung his bat with what witnesses described as equal parts elation and disdain.76 Three tying or go-ahead hits in one postseason game: only Sandy Alomar Jr. in 1997, Steve Garvey in 1984 and George Brett in 1978 had done it before him. "That's Wild Bill," said the rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt. "Big knock after big knock. He's a dog."7 The insurance arrived in the eighth from Turang and Bauers, singles both, giving Milwaukee its first margin greater than two runs — in either direction — of the entire postseason.6

What followed the starter was, again, flawless: May, Romero, Uribe and Ashby retired every one of the 15 men they faced, five perfect innings, the most wholly perfect bullpen work any postseason game has recorded, and the relief corps' account for the month now shows a single earned run across six games.67 So Milwaukee, swept from this round by this opponent a year ago, carries a 2-0 lead west — a position from which clubs have claimed the series 79 times in 95 tries — having spent the enemy's two aces, Skubal and Yamamoto, for no return at all.6 The captain declines the laurel: "We haven't accomplished anything yet," said Yelich. "It was a good start. But still a long way to go." The third game goes Wednesday at eight o'clock Eastern at Dodger Stadium, where Los Angeles must decide, among other matters, whether their greatest batsman plays in it — a question the Lineup Desk takes up above.2

News Around the League

THE LINEUP DESK: THE GREATEST INSTRUMENT IN THE GAME MAY BE SET DOWN — LOS ANGELES WILL WEIGH RESTING OHTANI FOR THE THIRD GAME, THE WIRE REPORTS, AFTER TWO MONTHS OF HURTS HAVE DIMMED THE LAMP

The titleholders return home trailing and carrying a question no club has ever wished to ask. According to a report from Katie Woo and Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic, the Dodgers will discuss whether Shohei Ohtani should sit for Wednesday's third game — a sentence that would have read as satire in July and reads as arithmetic in October.9

The figures make the case the eyes have been making for weeks. Ohtani has managed lingering injuries to the right biceps and left knee since at least June, hurts that sent him to the injured list in September; across his last 35 games, regular season and postseason together, he has batted .197 with a .629 on-base-plus-slugging. He has not homered since August 18 — a drought of 110 plate appearances, the longest of his career — and this postseason stands 3-for-20 with seven strikeouts, dropped already from second in the order to the cleanup spot.9 "He doesn't feel great," the manager Dave Roberts told the reporting parties. "It's having a conversation with him tomorrow, kind of try to figure out what's best for him, what's best for us. He certainly has earned that conversation and deserves it."9

Should the conversation end in rest, the beneficiary would likely be Josue De Paula, ranked the game's fourth-finest prospect by MLB Pipeline's reckoning, who reached base in half of his 42 plate appearances after a September summons and has been confined this October to three pinch-hitting errands. His outfield glove being the acknowledged weakness, the young man's bat can enter the lineup only through the designated hitter's door — which is to say, only at Ohtani's expense.9 The Herald observes merely that October is the month in which even the grandest accounts come due, and that the titleholders' ledger now shows two debts and dwindling collateral.

THE CASUALTY DESK: TWO RAYS MEET AT SPEED BENEATH A FOUL FLY AND BOTH RISE TO TELL OF IT — CAMINERO TAKES THE BLOW IN THE CHEST AND KEEPS HIS POST, DeLUCA TAKES IT IN THE SHOULDER, AND TAMPA BAY EXHALES

The fright of the American opener outlasted its score. In the ninth inning Monday, Brayan Rocchio lifted a foul fly toward the Cleveland bullpen down the left-field line; Jonny DeLuca pursued it from his post in left, Junior Caminero ran back from third, and in the noise of 35,361 neither man heard the other coming. The ball fell untouched. The players did not — left shoulders absorbing most of a collision that sent DeLuca rolling into the bullpen bench and left Caminero seated against the low wall in evident pain.10

The reckoning, mercifully, was small. Caminero — struck mostly in the chest, he said, the headache "just kind of the normal aftereffect" — remained in the game and trotted back to third base while the dome's loudspeakers offered the theme from "Rocky." "I feel good. Feel good overall," he reported afterward. His manager Kevin Cash concurred: "I think he just got the wind knocked out of him, and he seems to be totally fine now." DeLuca owned to a banged-up shoulder and hand and expected no lasting trouble from either. "Just two guys going hard at it, and obviously it's pretty noisy," the outfielder shrugged. "I think Cami's good. I'm pretty good."10 The Rays, a run down in a series growing heavier by the evening, will take the diagnosis as the day's one unqualified victory.

THE HOMECOMING DESK: TONIGHT AT EIGHT, THE BOY FROM PLANT CITY TAKES THE HILL HE ONCE WATCHED FROM THE CHEAP SEATS — MESSICK, AGED SEVEN AT THE 2008 WORLD'S SERIES, FACES PERALTA, A MAN REMADE ON THE GULF SINCE AUGUST

The second game of the American League round, this evening at eight o'clock Eastern at Tropicana Field, prints two biographies on one card. Parker Messick was seven years old on October 23, 2008, when he watched from these very stands as the Rays took a World Series game from Philadelphia; tonight the left-hander from Plant City — a town he commends for its people, its food and its Strawberry Festival — starts a pennant-round game on that same floor, with family and friends in the seats and his hometown throwing a watch party besides. "I have so many good memories here," said the Guardians' young ace, who went 12-9 with a 2.56 earned-run average this season and has thrown 193 innings against a previous professional high of 138 1/3. "To be able to do it on this stage now is just an incredible opportunity."11 His last outing, an abbreviated 65-pitch start in the Division round, he waves off — "missed some pitches by tiny margins that ended up in walks" — and his fastball in it ran above his season's average velocity, which he offers as evidence the arm remains sound in October.11

Opposite him stands the resurrection. Freddy Peralta came to Tampa Bay from the Mets on August 2 carrying a 4.99 earned-run average from his 22 New York starts; on the Gulf he has been another pitcher entirely — a 3.25 figure in his Rays service, by the ledger, including a September of 0.96 across five starts — and in his Division-round outing he threw 65 percent fastballs at nearly 97 miles the hour, well above his season custom.1312 "What clicked is him coming over here and just flushing whatever had gone on," said Cash, "approaching it like a fresh start."12 The deadball desks will relish the footnote: Peralta spent his first eight seasons and nine postseason errands in the employ of Milwaukee — the very club now two games to the good in the other league's round — and tonight pitches to keep his own round from slipping to 2-0 before it leaves for Cleveland.12

THE QUARTERMASTER DESK: EACH SIDE SHUFFLES ONE CARD FOR THE PENNANT ROUND — CLEVELAND ADDS A THIRTEENTH ARM IN CECCONI, AND TAMPA BAY SUMMONS YOUNG HOPKINS, LATELY OF THE DEVELOPMENT LIST, WITH HIS HUNDRED-MILE BOLT

Both American League quartermasters amended their manifests before Monday's opener, and both amendments bought pitching. Cleveland added the right-hander Slade Cecconi and set down the utility man Daniel Schneemann, electing to carry 13 pitchers after a Division round that wrung the staff like wash — three games in four days, seven pitchers used in one and eight in another. "Having that 13th pitcher was really important to us," said Vogt, who prizes Cecconi — 21 starts this season before a late move to the bullpen — as a man who "can throw up to 40, 50 pitches" in a single errand. The cost is bench flexibility: the rookie Angel Genao now stands as the lone spare part across the middle infield.14

Tampa Bay's exchange was a reliever for a reliever and a story besides: the left-hander Garrett Cleavinger out, and in his place Brody Hopkins, a hard-throwing young right-hander who in early August sat on the development list at Triple-A Durham, learning the bullpen trade, and who now finds himself dressing for a Championship Series. His manager's commissioning speech was brief. "He just said, 'You ready to pitch?'" Hopkins recounted. "And I'm ready to pitch." The young man brings a fastball of triple-digit reputation and breaking stuff his employers describe in terms usually reserved for weather. "Going from the dev list to the ALCS in two months, it's pretty crazy to think about," he allowed. "I'm juiced and ready to go."15

THE DESERT DESK: THE FALL CIRCUIT HANDS OUT ITS FIRST LAURELS — FIVE HITS IN A DEBUT FOR CLEVELAND'S FRANCISCA, WHO BATTED .556 FOR THE WEEK, AND A FASTBALL OF A HUNDRED AND THREE FROM WASHINGTON'S SUSANA

From Arizona, where the game's apprentices play out October in the sunshine, the Fall League has named its first weekly honorees. Welbyn Francisca, a 20-year-old infielder in the Cleveland chain, announced himself with five hits in his very first game for the Surprise club and closed the week leading the circuit at .556 with a .944 slugging figure and seven runs driven in across four games — the continuation of a season in which he climbed three levels and struck 19 home runs in 79 games, finishing at Double-A Akron among the Eastern League's youngest men.16

The pitching laurel went to Jarlin Susana of the Washington chain, who struck out eight and allowed one earned run over 5 2/3 innings spanning two starts for Salt River — and who supplied the week's most emphatic single datum, a fastball registered at 103.8 miles the hour, paired with a slider spinning near 3,000 revolutions.16 Cleveland's October is otherwise occupied, as the rest of this number attests, and Washington's ended with the summer — but both nurseries, evidently, are in bloom.

Tonight the American League holds the floor alone — the second game at the dome at eight o'clock — while the National League travels; its third game goes Wednesday at eight at Dodger Stadium, and Thursday both rounds sit at once, Tampa Bay at Cleveland at six and Milwaukee at Los Angeles at nine.2 A reader keeping this month's ledger will have noticed its governing law: the clubs pronounced dead keep batting. Cleveland stood two defeats from winter a week ago Sunday and has not lost since; Milwaukee was swept from its round a year ago and now holds that same round by the lapels; and the titleholders' two aces have been spent without a win to show. The game honors no form sheet for long — that is its oldest kindness, and this paper's favorite. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE MIDNIGHT LESSON COMES DUE, AND THE BILL IS PRESENTED TO THE FINEST LEFT HAND IN THE LAND — TURANG, SCHOOLED IN AN EMPTY CAGE TWO NIGHTS PRIOR, CLOUTS SKUBAL THE OPPOSITE WAY; THE BOY LARA SINGLES HOME THE DIFFERENCE, AND FOUR RELIEVERS BAR THE DOOR ON THE CHAMPIONS: BREWERS 2, DODGERS 1 IN THE PENNANT OPENER
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 96 · Monday, the Twelfth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE MIDNIGHT LESSON COMES DUE, AND THE BILL IS PRESENTED TO THE FINEST LEFT HAND IN THE LAND — TURANG, SCHOOLED IN AN EMPTY CAGE TWO NIGHTS PRIOR, CLOUTS SKUBAL THE OPPOSITE WAY; THE BOY LARA SINGLES HOME THE DIFFERENCE, AND FOUR RELIEVERS BAR THE DOOR ON THE CHAMPIONS: BREWERS 2, DODGERS 1 IN THE PENNANT OPENER

The duel the statisticians ranked among the three finest ever printed on an October card resolves into something homelier and better: Misiorowski, missing his best stuff, opens with 11 straight fastballs and grinds 13 outs from 94 pitches; Skubal retires nine of his first ten with six strikeouts and then cannot miss a bat again; Brice Turang — 2-for-16 in the Division round until a late-night tutorial with the hitting coach straightened his path — golfs a 2-0 sinker 384 feet into the home bullpen, Luis Lara pokes the go-ahead single at 21 years of age, and Milwaukee's bullpen, 19 2/3 October innings without an earned run and counting, hands the defending champions a 2-1 verdict in Game 1 of a Championship Series they swept a year ago

The decisive blow of the National League's pennant opener was struck two nights before the game began, in an empty batting cage under American Family Field. Brice Turang had carried a 2-for-16 Division Series home from the San Diego round, and a 1-for-15 from last October's Championship Series before that, so he stayed late at the park with the hitting coach Daniel Vogelbach to sand his swing back down to its essentials — hands tight, path straight, the ball driven back up the middle. "That's what he was working on, exactly," Pat Murphy would say afterward. "Instead of his hands dropping and cutting across, to just get straight to the baseball."6 On Sunday evening, before 42,617 at American Family Field, the homework was graded in public: Brewers 2, Dodgers 1, and the club that was swept out of this very round by this very opponent a year ago leads it, one game to none.

The advertised duel arrived imperfect and was the better theater for it. Jacob Misiorowski, the young ace who led all baseball in earned-run average this summer, confessed afterward he "didn't think I had my best stuff," and the evidence agreed — the Dodgers fouled off 21 of the 42 swings they took at him and made him labor 35 pitches through the second inning alone, where a walk to Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages' single to right produced the visitors' lone run.43 But the young man opened the night with 11 consecutive fastballs, the first at 102.3 miles the hour to Mookie Betts and the warmest at 104.0 to Freddie Freeman, and when the second inning stood bases loaded with one out he coaxed from Kiké Hernández the double play that ended it — Cooper Pratt with the clean pick at short, Turang with the pivot.43 A disputed balk stretched his fourth; he answered by striking out Kyle Tucker. His final accounting — one run on five hits across four and a third innings, 94 pitches — was less a masterpiece than a load-bearing wall, raised by a pitcher who has thrown nearly 190 innings this year, "way over," his manager marvels, anything he had done before.4

Tarik Skubal, meanwhile, was for three innings everything his billing promised, retiring nine of the first ten Milwaukee men with six strikeouts. Then the lineup saw him a second time, and the spell broke with an audible snap: the Brewers swung and missed at better than half his offerings through three innings, and at precisely one pitch thereafter.5 In the fourth, Turang — who had just fouled a pitch off his own kneecap — got a 2-0 sinker in on the hands and did exactly what the midnight tutorial prescribed, staying inside the ball and driving it the opposite way, 384 feet to left-center into the home bullpen for the tie.63 "I wasn't trying to hit a homer," the second baseman said. "I was trying to hit a nice line drive back up the middle." The pitcher tipped his cap — "in the zone, but it's in," Skubal allowed, "a good swing" — and then undid himself in the fifth by the oldest sin in the book, a leadoff walk to Garrett Mitchell. "The leadoff walk just can't happen," Skubal said plainly. Pratt bunted the runner along, and Luis Lara, the 21-year-old in right field, lined the first-pitch changeup he saw into center for the lead.53 Skubal's five innings and 81 pitches made the shortest of his eight postseason starts.5

What remained was the machinery Milwaukee trusts most. DL Hall faced exactly one batter and got two outs for his trouble, inducing the double play that erased Betts in the fifth; Abner Uribe took the sixth, Aaron Ashby the seventh and eighth, and Trevor Megill the ninth, where he complicated matters with two walks before Betts drove a ball to the deepest part of center that Mitchell ran down at the warning track to end it.34 The relief corps' October ledger now reads 19 2/3 innings without an earned run among Hall, Uribe, Ashby and Megill, a bullpen earned-run average of 0.38 through five games — tied for the third-lowest any club has carried through its first five postseason contests since 1969 — and opposing batsmen at a .163 figure.4 "We saw their four leverage guys tonight," Dave Roberts said, "and we just couldn't muster anything." His offense has two hits in 27 plate appearances with runners in scoring position this October, both of them Pages'.5 "At some point," said Betts, "we've got to get ours."3

The ledger notes what the evening portends. Every one of Milwaukee's five October games has been settled by one or two runs, and the two runs it scored Sunday are more than it managed in any single game of last autumn's Championship Series sweep.37 History leans gently toward the winner: clubs taking Game 1 of a best-of-seven have claimed the series 127 times in 197 tries.3 But the champions' answer arrives with scarcely a pause — the second sitting is this very evening at five o'clock Eastern, Yoshinobu Yamamoto against the rookie Logan Henderson, and the account of that matchup is taken up elsewhere in this number.2

News Around the League

THE WAKING DESK: VOGT PROMISED AN ANSWER UPON RISING, AND THE ANSWER IS GRIFFIN — THE WELL-TRAVELED LEFT HAND, THREE YEARS IN JAPAN AND AN ALL-STAR AT LAST, OPENS THE PENNANT ROUND AGAINST RASMUSSEN AND THE RESTED RAYS AT EIGHT O'CLOCK TONIGHT

When Stephen Vogt was asked Saturday night, amid the champagne, who would pitch the Championship Series opener, he laughed that he would let the world know when he woke up. He woke, and the ball belongs to Foster Griffin. "It was a no-brainer to give the ball to Foster in Game 1," the manager said Sunday, and the pitcher called the assignment "a huge honor" before declining all sentiment: "I feel like there's still a job to be done."9

The choice is a story the deadball desks would have relished. Griffin returned to these shores only this season after three years' employment in Japan, made his first All-Star team, posted a 3.06 earned-run average across 22 starts for Washington, and crossed to Cleveland at the August trade deadline, where a single eight-run calamity against Baltimore inflated an otherwise respectable ledger — a 3.73 figure over his other eight starts, and seven strikeouts in 2 2/3 innings of Division Series relief since.9 The arithmetic behind the romance is colder: Parker Messick and Gavin Williams, the co-aces who spent everything in the five-game escape from Chicago, are not on regular rest until the second and third games, and the Rays batted a league-handsome .752 by on-base-plus-slugging against right-handed pitching this season but a .679 against left — 25th in the game. Cleveland sends the left hand.9

Opposite him at eight o'clock Eastern at Tropicana Field stands Drew Rasmussen, rested to the point of luxury, who carried a no-hitter into the eighth inning of his last start and who threw seven scoreless at this same Cleveland club in July, allowing one hit.8 The season series went 5-1 to Tampa Bay; the two clubs between them carry the sport's longest waits, Cleveland without a championship since 1948 and the Rays without one in their 28 years of existence — the matter this paper took up at length yesterday, and which begins settling itself tonight.8

THE REJOINDER DESK: NO REST FOR THE BEATEN — YAMAMOTO, WHO THREW NINE FULL INNINGS AT MILWAUKEE IN LAST YEAR'S ROUND, TAKES THE BALL AT FIVE O'CLOCK AGAINST A ROOKIE WHO HAS NEVER ONCE BEEN BATTERED

The champions' opportunity for redress arrives before the sting fades: Game 2 goes this evening at five o'clock Eastern in Milwaukee, and Los Angeles sends the surest thing October has lately known. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, the reigning World Series Most Valuable Player, carries a 2.14 postseason earned-run average and has won all but one of his 11 postseason starts; in this very fixture a year ago — Game 2 of the Championship Series, in this very ballpark — he threw the first complete game of his American career, and in the Division round just concluded he allowed Atlanta one run across seven innings.7

Milwaukee's answer is Logan Henderson, 24 years old, who has made 24 starts in the major leagues and never in any of them allowed more than three runs — and who, the Milwaukee faithful will note with relish, outdueled Tarik Skubal at Dodger Stadium in August over a career-high seven innings.7 The undercard of anxieties favors the home nine as well: Will Smith stands 1-for-19 this October with seven strikeouts, Ohtani bats lower in the order than the world is accustomed to seeing him, and the champions' timeliest hitting remains the property of Andy Pages alone.7

The statisticians append the grandest framing: this is only the 17th postseason meeting of two 100-win clubs, the sixth in a Championship round, and the National League has seen exactly one such series before — Philadelphia and Cincinnati, in 1976.7 The argument removes to Los Angeles for Wednesday's third game.2

THE INFIRMARY DESK: THE RAYS SHEATHE McCLANAHAN FOR THE WINTER — NOT HURT, SAYS CASH, MERELY SPENT, AND THE CLUB DECLINES TO SPEND HIM FURTHER

One subtraction from the American League card before it begins: Shane McClanahan will not pitch again this year. The left-hander has not worked since the 3rd of September, when forearm tightness ended a start against Texas, and Kevin Cash announced Sunday that the club has shut him down for the balance of the postseason — with the emphatic clarification that this is prudence, not calamity. "Shane is done for the season," the manager said. "He's a healthy pitcher."10

The caution is easily understood by anyone who has read the man's medical file: a second reconstruction of the elbow, then a nerve injury in the triceps that cost him 2025 under the knife, two and a half seasons surrendered to the arm before this year's return — 10 wins against 7, a 3.36 earned-run average, 106 strikeouts in 118 innings across 24 starts. His manager nominates him for the game's comeback laurels, an advocacy this paper records as advocacy, the ballots being months from counted.10 McClanahan remains with the club through October in the capacity Cash describes as "being the best teammate"; the Rays will prosecute the pennant round with the rotation that needed no asterisk — Rasmussen tonight, with Freddy Peralta, Nick Martinez, and one of Griffin Jax or Ian Seymour behind him.10

THE MARKET DESK: JAZZ CHISHOLM TAKES HIS ONE-AND-FORTY STOLEN BASES TO THE AUCTION HOUSE — THE WIRE SURVEYS THE BIDDERS, AND THE GULF BETWEEN ASKING AND APPRAISAL WOULD SWALLOW A FRANCHISE

The winter market stirs even as October plays on. The wire this weekend surveyed the free agency of Jazz Chisholm Jr., the Yankees' second baseman, who arrives at the auction a 29-year-old by next Opening Day, with a season of .231, 19 home runs, and a career-high 41 stolen bases, third-most in the American League, worth some three and a half wins above replacement by the modern accounting.11 The survey names the Tigers, Blue Jays, Angels, Padres and Reds as plausible suitors, a return to the Bronx not excluded, and notes the strikeouts — 157 of them, a whiff rate in the game's bottom tier — that keep the appraisers' enthusiasm in check.11

The arithmetic of the bargaining table is where the entertainment lies. An executive consulted by the wire projects three or four years at about $20 million per annum; the player's camp, by an earlier report the wire recalls, has floated eight to ten years at $35 million. The Herald, whose sympathies in matters of the purse are a matter of standing record, begrudges no workingman a bold opening price — the owners' side of these tables has never once undersold itself — and merely observes that between those two figures lies a winter's worth of negotiating, which this paper will follow with its customary interest.11

October presents its first two-sitting evening of the pennant rounds: the National League's second game at five o'clock Eastern in Milwaukee, the American League's first at eight at Tampa Bay's dome — a reader with a wireless set and no other obligations may take in both, and this paper recommends the indulgence. Tuesday the American League argument continues at the dome at eight; Wednesday the National League's removes to Los Angeles.2 Yesterday this desk counseled its readers to be seated early for Skubal against Misiorowski, and the counsel stands vindicated in an unexpected key — the finest pairing the card could print was decided not by either famous arm but by a second baseman's midnight homework and a bullpen that has yet to surrender an earned run all month. The game keeps its own counsel; that is why we keep buying tickets. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: ONE-AND-TWENTY STRIKEOUTS IN THE DRIZZLE AND A HOMER GOLFED FROM THE GRASSTOPS — WILLIAMS FANS TWELVE ON TWO DAYS' REST, RAMÍREZ SUPPLIES THE ONLY RUNS FROM BENEATH HIS OWN KNEES, AND CLEVELAND, TWO GAMES DEAD ON MONDAY, PACKS FOR THE PENNANT ROUND: GUARDIANS 2, WHITE SOX 0
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 95 · Sunday, the Eleventh of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

ONE-AND-TWENTY STRIKEOUTS IN THE DRIZZLE AND A HOMER GOLFED FROM THE GRASSTOPS — WILLIAMS FANS TWELVE ON TWO DAYS' REST, RAMÍREZ SUPPLIES THE ONLY RUNS FROM BENEATH HIS OWN KNEES, AND CLEVELAND, TWO GAMES DEAD ON MONDAY, PACKS FOR THE PENNANT ROUND: GUARDIANS 2, WHITE SOX 0

The decider by the lake is settled by the two oldest instruments in Cleveland's kit — pitching, and José Ramírez: Gavin Williams, 48 hours removed from the first relief errand of his life, carries a no-hitter into the sixth and strikes out 12 to tie Charles Nagy's franchise postseason mark, the staff entire fans 21 Chicago batsmen, the most ever recorded in a nine-inning game of any month in the game's history, and Ramírez reaches down for a knuckle curve nine inches off the ground — the lowest pitch ever hit for a postseason homer in the tracking era — and barely clears the right-field wall with the two runs that make Cleveland the 11th club ever to climb from two games down in a best-of-five, the first since 2017, with the Rays waiting at their dome Monday night

The rain never quite stopped at Progressive Field on Saturday night, and neither did the strikeouts. Before 36,889 umbrella-minded believers, in a steady 65-degree drizzle, the fifth and deciding game of the American League Division Series resolved itself into the two commodities Cleveland has trusted since the deadball days — unhittable pitching and José Ramírez — and two hours and thirty-six minutes after the first pitch the scoreboard read Guardians 2, White Sox 0, the series 3 games to 2, and the season, for one of the Central's two quarrelsome neighbors, over.

Gavin Williams had called for this baseball. As this paper set down yesterday morning, the big right-hander closed Thursday's Game 4 with the first relief appearance of his professional life, then stopped by his manager's office to claim the Game 5 start he was always scheduled to make; the club hoped the 18-pitch cameo would read, in the final accounting, as a high-intensity side session. It read as prophecy. Williams faced one man over the minimum through three innings, struck out the side in the fourth, and did not permit a hit until Kyle Teel's two-out single in the sixth — a lone single, two walks and a hit batsman the whole of Chicago's account against him, with 12 strikeouts beside, his four-seamer averaging 99.1 miles the hour against a regular-season mean of 97.6.4 The dozen ties Charles Nagy's 1996 mark for the most in a postseason game in the franchise's books, and stands one shy of the winner-take-all record Tarik Skubal set only last October.4 When a walk to Miguel Vargas loaded the bases with two out in the sixth, Williams left to a standing ovation — "He ran out of pitches," said Stephen Vogt. "That's the only reason he came out of that game" — and Erik Sabrowski fanned Munetaka Murakami on five pitches to end the threat.4 The researchers of the Elias Bureau append the filigree: Williams is only the third pitcher in postseason history to record the final out of one game and start the next with elimination hanging over both, after Mordecai Brown in 1910 and Hank Borowy in 1945 — and the only one of the three whose club won the second game.5

The runs, both of them, belonged to the captain. At 9:03 by the Eastern clock the "Jo-sé! Jo-sé!" chant rolled around the grandstand; at 9:04, with Steven Kwan aboard and two strikes on him in the fourth, Ramírez reached down for Sean Burke's 78-mile-an-hour knuckle curve — a pitch measured at 0.74 feet above the earth, the lowest any man has hit for a postseason home run since the tracking instruments arrived in 2008, and the lowest of Ramírez's own career besides — and golfed it 348 feet to right, where it cleared the wall by a courtesy.65 The building shook, the lights flickered, and the crowd sang him out of the dugout for a curtain call. The man himself dismissed the pitch-classification sciences entirely: "Come on! You know! It was a home run pitch!"6 He is the first Cleveland batsman ever to homer in consecutive postseason games with elimination at stake in both, and his ledger since the series turned — 5-for-12, four extra-base hits, seven runs driven in across Games 3, 4 and 5, after an 0-for-6 beginning — is the whole story of the comeback in one line.63 "If there's one person on the planet I would not doubt, it's José Ramírez," said the club president Chris Antonetti; the reliever Sabrowski proposed, more economically, "Build the statue."3

And then there is the number that wants its own paragraph: 21. Williams, Sabrowski, Hunter Gaddis and the closer Cade Smith — the last two perfect across the final three innings, Smith collecting five outs for the save — struck out one-and-twenty Chicago batsmen, the most in any nine-inning game, regular season or postseason, in the recorded history of the major leagues. The previous postseason mark was 19, set in Game 3 of this very series, by this very staff.5 Cleveland's 75 strikeouts for the series are the most ever administered in a best-of-five, eleven clear of any other club's.5 Chicago's manager Will Venable declined every alibi: "I thought it was less about chase and more about being attacked in the zone... the story is just being able to put the ball in play."7 Burke, the losing pitcher, deserved kinder arithmetic — five innings, four hits, the two Ramírez runs his only blemish — and his manager called the fatal delivery "a good pitch, and obviously a better swing."6

So the Guardians stand as the 11th club in history to lose the first two games of a best-of-five and win it anyway, the first since the 2017 Yankees — who performed the trick, the records dryly note, in Cleveland — and just the fourth to do it after dropping the opening pair at home.5 A franchise that entered the evening 2-9 in win-or-go-home contests has now taken three straight elimination games, the same way it erased a five-and-a-half-game divisional deficit in September. "Backs against the wall!" Vogt hollered at the center of the clubhouse scrum, before the champagne interrupted him. "You boys showed up. You showed out... We've got eight more wins to go!"3 The first four are to be sought at Tampa Bay's dome, where the Championship Series opens Monday night at eight o'clock Eastern — the lakefront nine against the best record in the American League, 1948 against 1998, the two longest-suffering droughts left standing, and the account of it taken up elsewhere in this number.2

News Around the League

THE CURTAIN DESK: TONIGHT IN MILWAUKEE, A PAIRING SEEN THIRTEEN TIMES IN FIFTEEN HUNDRED OCTOBER GAMES — SKUBAL AND MISIOROWSKI, THE FIRST AND FOURTH ARMS IN ALL THE LAND, OPEN THE PENNANT ROUND AT EIGHT O'CLOCK

The National League's curtain rises this evening at eight o'clock Eastern at American Family Field, and the statisticians have done the arithmetic on what the ticket buys: a duel in the top one percent of all postseason pitching matchups of the last 55 years. By Baseball Savant's rolling measure of current form, Tarik Skubal is today the No. 1 pitcher in baseball and Jacob Misiorowski the No. 4 — and of the nearly 1,500 postseason starts since 1971, exactly 13 have paired two top-four arms against one another. Ranked by the average standing of the two starters, tonight ties for third-best ever, behind only Dwight Gooden against Mike Scott in the 1986 Championship Series — a 1-0 masterpiece in which Scott fanned 14 — and Roger Clemens against Dave Stewart in 1990.8

The particulars want little embroidery beyond what this paper has carried all week. Misiorowski, 16-5, led the entire major leagues in earned-run average (1.80), strikeouts (252), walks-and-hits per inning (0.80) and opponents' batting mark (.157), and against these same Dodgers owns a 1.59 figure across three career meetings; Skubal, the twice-laureled Cy Young man acquired from Detroit at the Deadline, carries a 1.97 earned-run average over seven career postseason starts into the assignment.98 It is 103 wins against 100, the league's two best outfits, a rematch of last autumn's Championship Series — swept by Los Angeles — and the third such meeting since 2018. "When we play our brand of baseball... we're a really hard team to beat," says Christian Yelich; the Milwaukee faithful will add, sotto voce, that their club declined to be the highest bidder for Skubal in July, and that the risk of exactly this evening was the price of the prudence.98

The margins of the card: Los Angeles frets over cold bats — Shohei Ohtani at .154 this October and Will Smith at .063 — while William Contreras, who led the majors in runs driven home in September, arrives slashing .375 for the Division round; the Dodgers' infirmary lists Blake Treinen as unlikely for the postseason, while Milwaukee reports itself whole.9 And the schedule holds one more enticement: both aces stand lined up to meet again in a potential fifth game at Los Angeles.8 The second sitting is Monday at five o'clock Eastern, before the series removes west for Wednesday's third.2

THE DOME DESK: MONDAY AT THE TROP, THE TWO LONGEST WAITS IN THE LEAGUE SIT DOWN TOGETHER — RASMUSSEN LIKELY FOR THE RESTED RAYS, WHILE VOGT PROMISES HIS OWN STARTER UPON WAKING

The American League's pennant round convenes Monday night at eight o'clock Eastern at Tropicana Field, and it is a meeting of the sport's two most patient congregations: Cleveland has not won the World Series since 1948, Tampa Bay never in the 28 years since the franchise first took the artificial turf — and one of the two is now guaranteed a seat at the Fall Classic table should it win four games.102

The pitching ledgers could scarcely be less alike. The Rays, idle since Wednesday's sweep of New York, have their ace Drew Rasmussen lined up for the opener on extended rest — his last outing carried a no-hitter into the eighth inning — and a bullpen so little used in the Division round that the closer Bryan Baker worked every game with a day's rest besides.10 Cleveland, by contrast, spent everything by the lake on Saturday: Gavin Williams is unlikely before Thursday's third game, Parker Messick before Tuesday's second, and when Stephen Vogt was asked who takes the ball Monday, the manager laughed and said, "I'll let you know when I wake up tomorrow" — the plausible candidates being Tanner Bibee, the opener Daniel Espino, Joey Cantillo and Foster Griffin.10

The bloodlines cross in every direction, as they will among the league's thrifty houses: Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Kevin Kelly all began as Cleveland chattel; Kevin Cash coached Cleveland's bullpen before his long tenancy in the Tampa Bay dugout; Vogt's own playing career opened 0-for-27 in a Rays uniform. The season series went 5-1 to Tampa Bay, 20 runs to 8, with half the meetings settled by a single run — these clubs pitch, catch the ball, and beat nobody but each other's patience.10 The ceremonial first ball Monday is entrusted to Carl Crawford, of the 2008 pennant winners.10

THE VALEDICTORY DESK: THE SOUTH SIDE FOLDS ITS TENTS WITH WET EYES AND A FULL SCRAPBOOK — FROM A HUNDRED LOSSES THRICE RUNNING TO A GAME 5, AND A CLUBHOUSE VOWING ITS RETURN

The visiting clubhouse at Progressive Field held the usual October inventory — tears, embraces, and the chairman at the door. Jerry Reinsdorf stood and thanked his White Sox man by man as they came off the field, the proprietor's acknowledgment of a season nobody ordered: a club that lost 100 games in each of the three preceding summers seized the league's final Wild Card, swept Houston from the bracket, led the mighty by two games in this series, and died at last by the strikeout, 21 of them on the final night, 75 across the five games.7

The elegies were defiant. "It was fun, but we didn't want to end it here," managed the second baseman Chase Meidroth, through some difficulty. "They pitched their asses off. They deserve to go to the next round. It sucks, but we'll be back." Munetaka Murakami, four times a strikeout victim on the night, called the club "still a very young team" and the loss a lesson for carrying forward; the right-hander Mike Vasil put the house position plainest: "This team will be back. There's no denying that. But we made a lot of people believe... White Sox baseball is back and we are here to stay."7

The ledger supports the optimism better than the obituary suggests. Chicago led the American League in runs (776) and walks (589) this season and stood third in home runs (211); it never lost more than four games running all year; and the core of the enterprise is young enough that the autumn reads as a down payment rather than a squandering. The franchise's winner-take-all record now stands 0-2 across its long history — and the Herald, which watched this club make the summer far more interesting than anyone contracted for, suspects that particular ledger will get further entries soon enough.7

THE FRONT-OFFICE DESK: THE ATHLETICS' PRESIDENCY GOES BEGGING — FULD OF THE PHILADELPHIAS DECLINES THE CROWN, AND A BOSTON MAN STANDS NEXT IN THE ANTEROOM

Word from the executive corridors, where October is hiring season for everyone eliminated from it: Sam Fuld, the general manager of the Phillies, has declined an offer to become the Athletics' president of baseball operations, by the account of ESPN's sources. The suitors move down their list — Taylor Smith, an assistant general manager with the Red Sox, remains a leading candidate for the post.11

The Herald reads the refusal without astonishment. The Athletics, lately of Sacramento and bound eventually for Las Vegas, are offering a grand title attached to a franchise between addresses; Mr. Fuld, by contrast, already holds a chair in a contending organization. That the club's search now turns toward Boston's front office is noted here for the winter record — the game's executive carousel rarely stops turning once the first chair is declined.

The paper begrudges nobody a breath, but October grants none: tonight at eight by the Eastern clock the National League's argument opens in Milwaukee, Skubal against Misiorowski, a pairing the statisticians rank among the three finest ever printed on a postseason card; Monday the American League's opens at Tampa Bay's dome at eight, with the senior circuit's second sitting at five o'clock the same evening.2 Yesterday this paper observed that one of the game's two long waits — Cleveland's or Chicago's — would grow a day shorter by nightfall. It was Cleveland's, by the margin of a pitch nine inches off the ground. The Herald will be at its post for all of it. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: Postseason Off-Day Edition — the Tenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 94 · Saturday, the Tenth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

No contests this day; the pennant races rest.

0 days until the fifth and deciding game of the Division Series — the White Sox at the Guardians, eight o'clock this very evening by the lake (Saturday, the 10th of October, 2026).

News Around the League

THE DECIDER DESK: ONE QUARREL LEFT OF FOUR, AND IT ENDS TONIGHT BY THE LAKE — WILLIAMS KEEPS THE BALL HE NEVER SURRENDERED, BURKE TAKES IT WITH NO OPENER AHEAD OF HIM, AND THE WINNER PACKS FOR TAMPA BAY

The bracket has spent its riches down to a single argument. Of October's four Division Series, three are settled and their winners gone to their rest; only the Central's remains, and it concludes this very evening — the White Sox at the Guardians, eight o'clock Eastern at Progressive Field, the survivor to present itself at Tampa Bay's dome on Monday.26 Two games apiece, and the series' peculiar signature holds to the last: every victory in it has been taken in the other man's yard, Chicago seizing the first pair by the lake, Cleveland the next two on the South Side.

Stephen Vogt has answered the question his own Game 4 adventures raised: Gavin Williams — who closed Thursday's 9-5 verdict with the first relief errand of his professional life — keeps the start he was always scheduled to make, on his regular rest. "Gavin wants the ball," said the manager. "We want him to have the ball, and it's his game." The pitcher himself declines the taxonomy altogether: "It doesn't matter the role at this point," he offers, and reports the body sound. The Forest City nine hope Thursday's three-out cameo reads, in the final accounting, as a high-intensity side session rather than a withdrawal from tonight's funds.3

Chicago counters with Sean Burke, 11-7 with a 3.34 mark on the year, and this time no opener precedes him — the assignment is his from the first pitch. His Game 2 turn in bulk relief, one run on one hit across five and a third innings with six strikeouts and thirteen men retired in order at one stretch, remains the finest pitching the visitors have shown Cleveland all series, and Will Venable pronounces him "built for these types of moments."4 The bullpen ledgers counsel economy on both sides of the field: Erick Fedde's 61 pitches of Thursday likely rule him out of tonight's account, Hagen Smith has now worked three times in the series and on consecutive days, and Grant Taylor — charged with four runs of Thursday's sixth without recording an out — professes himself ready for anything at all. "We just want to win this series however possible," says Venable, "and wherever that is, we'll take it."4 The stakes have stood in this paper's columns all week and want no embroidery this morning: the Pale Hose chase a first pennant round since 2005, the Guardians the lifting of the game's longest-standing championship drought, and one of those long waits grows one day shorter tonight.

THE ROTATION DESK: YESTERDAY'S SURMISE BECOMES TODAY'S OFFICIAL RECORD — SKUBAL SUNDAY AND YAMAMOTO MONDAY FOR LOS ANGELES, WHILE MILWAUKEE KEEPS ITS OWN COUNSEL

What this paper carried yesterday as the wire's well-reasoned surmise is now the official record: Dave Roberts on Friday named Tarik Skubal for Sunday's opening game in Milwaukee and Yoshinobu Yamamoto for Monday's second, precisely the order the reasoning foretold — Yamamoto proceeding on his accustomed five days of rest, with a sixth game held open for his return should the quarrel stretch so far.5 Milwaukee, for its part, has signed nothing: Jacob Misiorowski appears set to answer Skubal in the opener, but the Brewers have made no announcement, and the Herald reports the probability as a probability and not a fixture.5

The ledger behind the Los Angeles order is briefly told. In the Division round the four starters — Skubal, Blake Snell, Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow — allowed 4 earned runs in 21 1/3 innings among them, a 1.69 figure; Skubal's National League debut ran six innings of one-run work against Atlanta, and Yamamoto's Game 3 ran seven with 10 strikeouts.5 Behind the confirmed pair the projections place Snell third, on extended rest and still nursing the groin tightness that has trailed him since the middle of September — it showed in a ragged five-walk outing that lasted under four innings in Game 2 — and Glasnow fourth, in whose seven postseason starts the Boys in Blue have yet to taste defeat.5

The curtain rises Sunday at eight o'clock Eastern in Milwaukee, the second sitting follows Monday at five, and the argument removes to Los Angeles for Wednesday's third.2

THE REPOSE DESK: ELEVEN IDLE DAYS AGAINST THREE OF WORK — THE GULF COAST CLUB SCRIMMAGES AGAINST ITSELF THIS AFTERNOON WHILE OCTOBER CHOOSES ITS NEXT OPPONENT

The Rays, their sweep of New York concluded Wednesday, have made an art of the interval. Home Thursday and the rest of the day off; a full dress workout Friday at their dome; an intrasquad scrimmage this very afternoon, the club's hitters and pitchers obliged to make do with one another; a standard drill Sunday — and then Monday night, the first game of the pennant round, against whichever club survives tonight by the lake.6 Between the regular-season finale of September 27 and that first pitch the club will have counted eleven idle days against three of work. Kevin Cash accounts the rest a "privilege," and his charge to the room wants no translation: "We've got two more bites — two more bites on the bone!"6

The pitching plan waits politely upon tonight's result — "some pretty good ideas," the manager allows, with nothing final until the opponent is known — though Drew Rasmussen stands in line for the opener, as he stood for the Division round's, and Cash means to lean on the same five starters throughout.6 The repose has been kindest to the relief corps: Bryan Baker, the locksmith of the ninth of whom this paper wrote only yesterday, was used but sparingly in the sweep, as were Cam Booser and Kevin Kelly, and the Championship Series calendar — off days after the second and fifth games only — will ask considerably more of them than the Division round ever did.6

THE BALLOT DESK: TEN NAMES TO A LEAGUE AND TWO DAYS LEFT AT THE BOX — THE AARON HONOR NAMES ITS FINALISTS, FIVE OF THEM STILL AT THEIR DAY'S WORK THIS OCTOBER

The season's first ballot-box stands open. The Hank Aaron Award, the annual laurel for each league's most accomplished batsman, has its finalists for 2026: ten names to a league, selected by a committee of MLB.com's own journalists, with the winners to be chosen by a panel of the game's legends and past honorees — the fandom casting its own votes besides, at the league's site, until 11:59 Monday morning by the Eastern clock.7 The winners are to be announced November 11 at Las Vegas on the MLB Network's awards evening. The Herald, by its standing rule, reports a ballot as a ballot: nothing has yet been won, and the trophy keeps to its case until the panel speaks.

The rolls reward a reading. The American League's ten include Bobby Witt Jr., Riley Greene, Pete Alonso and Yordan Alvarez; the National's, Shohei Ohtani, Kyle Schwarber, Pete Crow-Armstrong and Fernando Tatis Jr.7 And five of the twenty are still in uniform this October: Junior Caminero and Yandy Díaz of Tampa Bay's waiting company, Miguel Vargas of the White Sox — at liberty to add to his argument this very evening — and Ohtani and Milwaukee's Jake Bauers, whose clubs open the pennant round against one another Sunday.7

THE PACIFIC DESK: NINE-AND-THIRTY CIRCUIT CLOUTS AND THE THREE JEWELS OF THE CENTRAL LEAGUE — SATO OF THE HANSHIN TIGERS WEARS JAPAN'S TRIPLE CROWN, AND THE POSTING WINDOW BECKONS

From the far shore of the Pacific comes word of a coronation. Teruaki Sato of the Hanshin Tigers has won the Japanese Central League's Triple Crown, batting .306 with 39 home runs and 106 runs driven across — a .991 on-base-plus-slugging besides — making him the ninth man in Nippon Professional Baseball's long history to lead his league in all three columns at once, and the first since Munetaka Murakami turned the trick for Yakult four years ago.89 The 27-year-old left-handed slugger, principally a third baseman, follows a 2025 campaign of 40 home runs and 102 runs batted in with the finest season of his life.9

What follows is the portion that concerns the thirty clubs of this hemisphere: the wire expects Sato posted for their inspection as soon as early November, and the insider Jon Heyman already names the Mets, the Yankees, the Phillies and the Dodgers among the likely bidders.8 The precedent travels well and sits near at hand — Murakami, the last man to wear this crown, crossed the ocean and now draws his pay from the White Sox, whose season comes to its winner-take-all hearing this very evening. The scouting reports will make their winter rounds; the Herald merely notes that the market for Japanese royalty has lately been a seller's.

The Friday ledger is a blank page — not a pitch thrown from one coast to the other — and the paper begrudges the quiet nothing, for the calendar now owes us riches on consecutive evenings: tonight at eight by the lake, the only fifth game October's first round produced; Sunday at eight, the National League's curtain in Milwaukee; Monday, the American League's at Tampa Bay's dome, with the senior circuit's second sitting at five o'clock the same day.2 Somewhere tonight a season ends in Cleveland — one or the other must — and a pennant argument gains its final party before the morning. The Herald will have the whole account in its next number. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
