entry.title: TEN MEN TO THE PLATE AND THE SIXTH INNING TAKES THE SOUTH SIDE'S VOICE AWAY — BAILEY RISES FROM THE BENCH TO STRIKE TWICE, RAMÍREZ CARRIES THE FLAME, AND CLEVELAND, TWICE LEFT FOR DEAD IN THIS SERIES, HAULS THE QUARREL HOME FOR A FIFTH AND FINAL SITTING: GUARDIANS 9, WHITE SOX 5
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 93 · Friday, the Ninth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 1 contest from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

TEN MEN TO THE PLATE AND THE SIXTH INNING TAKES THE SOUTH SIDE'S VOICE AWAY — BAILEY RISES FROM THE BENCH TO STRIKE TWICE, RAMÍREZ CARRIES THE FLAME, AND CLEVELAND, TWICE LEFT FOR DEAD IN THIS SERIES, HAULS THE QUARREL HOME FOR A FIFTH AND FINAL SITTING: GUARDIANS 9, WHITE SOX 5

The question Stephen Vogt put to his men before the Chicago leg — whether it is sweeter to madden 40,000 or to hush them — receives its answer in a six-run sixth: held to one hit and trailing 2-0 through four, the Cleveland nine draw level on Patrick Bailey's homer from the bench and José Ramírez's two-run drive, surrender the lead within the half-inning, then send ten batters against the Chicago relay — Bazzana's double past a diving Montgomery, two walks, four singles, and Grant Taylor, the four-inning savior of Game 1, retired not a single man — while Gavin Williams, the putative Game 5 starter, takes the last three outs of a 9-5 verdict that squares the only Division Series to reach a deciding game, Saturday at eight o'clock by the lake, the winner to call upon Tampa Bay on Monday

Stephen Vogt spent the week posing his club a riddle of acoustics. “What do you like better?” the Cleveland manager asked his men before the series removed to the South Side. “Do you like to make 50,000 people go crazy, or do you like to shut 50,000 people up? They're both very different feelings, but they're equally as fun.”3 On Thursday evening at Rate Field, before 39,920 believers dressed in black, the Guardians chose the second feeling, and the sixth inning administered it.

For four innings the evening leaned Chicago's way. The hosts manufactured two runs in the third by the humblest means October knows — Munetaka Murakami's bases-loaded walk and Sam Antonacci's sacrifice fly — while Cleveland managed a single hit and Parker Messick, the rookie left-hander entrusted with the season, walked four men and was gone after two and a third innings. The advertised duel of southpaws dissolved on both ends: Hagen Smith, Chicago's announced starter, lasted two outs and three walks himself, and the game passed into the hands of the two bullpens, where Erick Fedde held Cleveland quietly for three and two-thirds in bulk relief.

The fifth inning turned the ledger over. Patrick Bailey, who had begun the evening on the bench, lined a homer into the right-field seats; two batters on, José Ramírez — whose October revival this paper has chronicled daily — turned on a fly ball to right-center for a two-run clout and a 3-2 lead. Chicago answered in kind and at once, an Antonacci hit-by-pitch forcing in one run and Brenton Doyle's sacrifice fly another, and at 4-3 the home crowd permitted itself to believe. Then came the sixth. Angel Martínez was struck by a pitch, stole second, and scored when Travis Bazzana's double dropped just beyond the dive of right fielder Braden Montgomery — the groan from the grandstand was audible on the wireless — and the next six Cleveland batters all reached against Grant Taylor, the same Taylor whose four-inning save had stolen Game 1. Bailey singled, Rocchio and Kwan walked, and Ramírez, DeLauter and Adell singled in succession: ten men to the plate, six runs across, 9-4, and Taylor charged with four of them without recording an out. The researchers note the six-run frame ties the third-largest inning in Cleveland's postseason history, and that the franchise has now scored nine runs in consecutive October contests for only the second time, the first being Games 3 and 4 of the 1997 World Series.3

Miguel Vargas supplied the South Side's coda, a parting shot to left in the ninth, and it fell to Gavin Williams — the presumptive Game 5 starter, making the first relief appearance of his professional life — to take the final three outs on 18 pitches.4 That economy now hangs over Saturday: Cleveland's pitching plans for the decider are frankly unsettled, Messick's abbreviated start having forced seven relievers into service. “I'm good to go,” Williams offered afterward. “If I've got to start, I'll start. If I come out of the 'pen, I'll come out of the 'pen. I'll do anything.” Chicago, by contrast, arrives with its best bulk man, Sean Burke, rested and ready.4

So a series that has refused every tidy script gets the ending it deserves: two games apiece, each club having won twice in the other's yard, Game 5 Saturday at eight o'clock Eastern at Progressive Field — the only Division Series of the four to go the distance.24 The arithmetic of history calls it a coin flip: of the eighteen prior clubs to drop the first two games of a best-of-five and win the next two, ten went on to take the fifth, and home teams in winner-take-all games stand 70-68 all-time.3 Cleveland, chasing the longest active championship drought in the game — no title since 1948 — could become only the fourth club to climb from two games down in a Division Series after losing the first pair at home. Chicago, which as this paper noted yesterday has still never shown its home crowd an October victory this fall, must now win its fifth straight road scrap of the autumn to reach a first pennant round since 2005. “We kind of let the home crowd down those first two games,” said Steven Kwan. “So hopefully it's another chance at redemption.”4 The winner's reward: the rested Rays, Monday, at their dome.

News Around the League

THE BARGAINING DESK: THE OWNERS SLIDE A PAPER ACROSS THE TABLE — A SEASON SHORN TO 154 GAMES, A MONDAY OF REST, A LONGER OCTOBER, AND THE TOP SEEDS TO CHOOSE THEIR OWN PREY

While the Division round supplied the week's noise, the quieter table got a new document. Major League Baseball's latest proposal to the players' union, delivered Thursday, would return the game to a 154-game schedule beginning in 2029 — a figure the sport kept almost without interruption from 1904 to 1960 — with a scheduled off-day every Monday, four split doubleheaders per club, and a season ending a week earlier. The Division Series would stretch from best-of-five to best-of-seven, and, most novel of all, the highest seeds would choose their opponents: the third seed selecting its Wild Card quarry immediately after the regular season, the first seed naming its Division Series foe once the Wild Card round concludes. The league stipulates that no downward adjustment would be made to salaries for the shorter season, with bonus and option thresholds scaled proportionally.5

The league's case, in the words of its spokesman Glen Caplin, rests on player health and spectacle alike: a weekly off-day “good for player health,” a new national broadcast window, “fewer weekday afternoon games, a longer Division Series and more opportunities to see the game's best pitchers on the biggest stage.” The proposal's own prose, it must be said, confesses the box office as candidly as the training room — the added October off-days are commended for “increasing ratings and enhancing the value of the sport's media rights,” and the 2029 commencement happens to coincide, to the year, with the start of the league's next national media agreements.5

The Herald's sympathies on matters of the purse are a matter of public record, and it weighs the paper accordingly. A weekly day of rest and a schedule shortened at full pay are concessions the workingman's side of this game has sought since the deadball days, and the paper credits them as genuine. The choosing-of-opponents is theater — bulletin-board material by design, as the league's own wire cheerfully admits — and theater sells at the gate and on the air, where the owners keep the till. No formal answer from the union had reached the wires consulted by this desk when the edition went to press; the Herald will read it, when it comes, with its customary interest.

THE OVERTURE DESK: SUNDAY'S CURTAIN IN MILWAUKEE PROMISES A DUEL FOR THE AGES — THE YOUNG FIREBALLER OF THE CREAM CITY AGAINST THE TWICE-LAURELED LEFT HAND OF LOS ANGELES

The National League's pennant quarrel opens Sunday evening at eight o'clock Eastern in Milwaukee, the second sitting follows Monday at five, and the argument removes to Los Angeles on Wednesday — a rematch of last autumn's Championship Series and a meeting of the league's first and second seeds.2 Neither club has formally named its Game 1 pitcher, but the wire finds every sign pointing to the matchup of dreams: Jacob Misiorowski against Tarik Skubal.6

The credentials require little embroidery. Misiorowski, the 24-year-old to whom Milwaukee entrusts its loudest evenings, finished the regular season atop the entire major leagues in earned-run average (1.80), strikeouts (252), walks-and-hits per inning (0.80) and opponents' batting average (.157), and in the Division round his fastball touched 104.8 miles the hour while averaging 101.2.6 Skubal, the two-time reigning Cy Young man of the American League,9 crossed leagues at midsummer in the blockbuster that made him a Dodger10 and scarcely broke stride — a 2.61 earned-run average in the Los Angeles colors despite surrendering 44 days of his summer to elbow surgery, and six innings of one-run work in his National League postseason debut against Atlanta. The wire's reasoning for the pairing is sound: Yoshinobu Yamamoto, the other candidate, worked Tuesday and would be on short rest Sunday; Monday suits him naturally.6

The scribes call it perhaps the finest Game 1 matchup the bracket could have drawn. The Herald, having watched both men terrorize the summer from opposite leagues, declines to argue, and counsels its readers only to be seated early.

THE PADLOCK DESK: THREE-AND-THIRTY SAVES WITHOUT A STUMBLE — BAKER, THE SELF-MADE LOCKSMITH OF THE NINTH, CARRIES THE GAME'S SUREST THING INTO THE PENNANT ROUND

While Tampa Bay rests and waits upon Saturday's survivor, the wire pauses over the man who shut each door of the Division round behind him. Bryan Baker, the 31-year-old All-Star in his first season as the Rays' closer, saved all three victories of the sweep of New York — ten batters faced, four strikeouts, one lone walk the only man to reach — and became just the fourth pitcher since the save entered the official ledger in 1969 to nail down each of his club's first three postseason games, joining Manny Corpas, Mark Wohlers and Dennis Eckersley. He is the only one of the four to do it without allowing a hit.7

The season behind the October is of a piece: 41 saves to share the major-league lead, a 1.44 earned-run average, a .161 opponents' mark, and — the figure that says the most — 33 consecutive save chances converted since the 17th of May, the longest such run in the franchise's books. All of it managed on two pitches, fastball and changeup, by a former Oriole the Rays did not even plan to employ as a traditional closer when spring camp broke. “He's a rock, man. He's a maniac,” testifies the veteran Nick Martinez; manager Kevin Cash puts it as a question — “Is there a team that should feel better than us?”7

The Herald notes one filigree the wire supplies: the man with whom Baker shares the save crown, at 41 apiece, is Cleveland's Cade Smith — who worked an inning in Thursday's Game 4, and who may yet bring the argument into the Championship Series in person, should Saturday by the lake fall the Guardians' way.7

THE NURSERY DESK: THE PASTIME RECRUITS FROM THE CRADLE — MR. FALLON TEACHES THE SMALLEST FANS THEIR FIRST WORDS, AND THE WORDS ARE 'DODGERS' AND 'YANKEES'

The game's longest campaign — the one for the next generation — opened a new front this week. Jimmy Fallon, the late-night host and best-selling author, has partnered with the league on two board books for the very youngest prospects: Your Baby's First Word Will Be Dodgers and Your Baby's First Word Will Be Yankees, illustrated with amiable farm animals by Miguel Ordóñez, to be published by Macmillan's Feiwel and Friends imprint on February 2, 2027, and available now for the pre-ordering.8

“Parents spend months trying to get their baby's first word to be 'Mama' or 'Dada,'” Mr. Fallon explains. “This book is for parents with bigger dreams.”8 The Herald observes without malice that of the two titles, one arrives rather better timed than the other — the Dodger infant may yet babble his first word during a third consecutive championship parade, while the Yankee household, its October concluded on Wednesday, has until spring to rehearse.

The travel trunks own this Friday — not a contest on the continent — and then the calendar crowds: Saturday at eight o'clock, the fifth and final sitting of Cleveland and Chicago by the lake; Sunday at eight, the National League's curtain rises in Milwaukee; Monday, the American League's opens at Tampa Bay while the senior circuit plays its second at five o'clock.2 One series alone of October's first four went the full distance, and it is the one between two clubs who met thirteen times in the summer, settled their division by a single game, and now cannot be told apart at two games apiece.4 The Herald knows better than to predict it, and would not spoil it if it could. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: A SPECTATOR'S HAND RETURNS TO THE RIGHT-FIELD STANDS AND THIS TIME THE COURT COLLECTS — MESA'S TWO-RUN BROADSIDE OFF FRIED STANDS AS THE DIFFERENCE, VOLPE'S TYING BLOW IS RULED DOWN TO A DOUBLE, AND TAMPA BAY SWEEPS NEW YORK FROM OCTOBER: RAYS 4, YANKEES 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 92 · Thursday, the Eighth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 4 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

A SPECTATOR'S HAND RETURNS TO THE RIGHT-FIELD STANDS AND THIS TIME THE COURT COLLECTS — MESA'S TWO-RUN BROADSIDE OFF FRIED STANDS AS THE DIFFERENCE, VOLPE'S TYING BLOW IS RULED DOWN TO A DOUBLE, AND TAMPA BAY SWEEPS NEW YORK FROM OCTOBER: RAYS 4, YANKEES 3

Thirty Octobers less a single evening after a boy of twelve turned a fly ball into Bronx scripture, the replay court reverses the old miracle — Anthony Volpe's apparent game-tying two-run wallop in the sixth is found to have met a spectator's glove over the field of play, worth one run and second base and nothing more — while Victor Mesa Jr., who had already answered Ryan Vilade's first October four-bagger with a two-run drive of his own off Max Fried, supplies the margin; Ian Seymour wins in relief of the opener Martinez, Baker locks the ninth, and the Rays claim the first three-games-and-out sweep of a best-of-five in franchise annals, their third Championship Series berth, with the Guardians-White Sox survivor due at their dome Monday

On the ninth of October, 1996, a twelve-year-old named Jeffrey Maier reached over the right-field fence of the old Yankee Stadium and knocked a fly ball of Derek Jeter's into the seats. The umpires called it a home run rather than the interference it plainly was; the Yankees tied the Orioles that evening, won the game, won the series, and in time won everything, while the boy was toasted in Manhattan and cursed in Baltimore.5 The National Pastime keeps its ledgers open a long while, and on Wednesday night — thirty years later, less one evening, in the same right-field corner of the Bronx — the account came due.

The situation was composed with an archivist's care. Sixth inning, New York trailing 4-2, George Lombard Jr. aboard, and Volpe lined a sinker from Griffin Jax deep to left-center, where it carried to the wall, over the leap of Victor Mesa Jr., and was signaled a game-tying home run. Then the modern instrument did what 1996 could not: the replay court found that a spectator had met the ball with his glove over the field of play, that it would neither have cleared the barrier nor been caught, and wrote the entry down as it deserved — an RBI double, one run in, 4-3.4 Even the aggrieved manager filed no true grievance. “I thought they got it right,” said Aaron Boone, which may stand as the evening's epitaph.

The game around the famous call was a taut and worthy thing. Tampa Bay scratched first in the third, Jonathan Aranda singling home DeLuca while Taylor Walls was cut down at the plate on a relay that traveled right field to first base to shortstop to catcher. Ben Rice — the one Yankee bat October never cooled — answered at once. Vilade, a name new to the postseason register, put the visitors ahead with the first October home run of his life in the fourth; Spencer Jones doubled the score level again. And in the sixth Mesa turned on Fried for the two-run drive to right-center that settled the business, the left-hander's second surrender of the night and his last.

From there the Tampa relay — Seymour, Jax, Booser, Kelly, Baker — carried the one-run verdict home, the staff fanning twelve New York batsmen in all, and when Trent Grisham went down swinging to end the ninth, the visitors' clubhouse became a dance hall for the third time in a fortnight. The sweep is the first Tampa Bay has ever administered in a series of five, and only the second ever suffered by the Yankees in one, the other dating to the Championship Series of 1980. The Rays, champions of their division for the first time in five years, advance to the third Championship Series in the franchise's history, where the survivor of Cleveland and Chicago will call upon them Monday.3

The scrapbook this paper watched New York take down from the shelf on Tuesday — the flip of 2001, the rally of 2017 — stayed shut. The Bronx offense managed seven hits on the final night and never once held the lead; its season ends in the Division round for want of swinging, as its manager conceded, and the winter's accounting, which began within minutes of the final strike, is taken up elsewhere in this number.

“There's two more bites on the bone for us,” said the reliever Nick Martinez amid the champagne, quoting his manager's arithmetic — eleven wins wanted, eight remaining.3 The Herald observes only that a franchise long praised for doing much with little has now done the hardest thing October asks: it has made the Yankees watch.

The Postseason Card

RAMÍREZ EMPTIES EVERY POCKET OF THE TOOLBOX AND CLEVELAND DECLINES THE BROOM — TWO TWO-OUT TRIPLES, NINETEEN STRIKEOUTS BY THE VISITING RELAY, AND THE LAKE ERIE MEN DRAG THE QUARREL TO A FOURTH EVENING: GUARDIANS 9, WHITE SOX 3

The cold order this paper weighed yesterday — seven hits in sixty-one at-bats — wakes all at once on the South Side: Kwan singles home the tying run, Adell clears the sacks with a two-out triple in a four-run third, and Ramírez, wrist be hanged, files a double, a triple, two runs, two runs driven home, a stolen base and a diving stop at third into a single afternoon's work, while seven Cleveland pitchers fan nineteen Chicago batsmen and the bullpen-made hosts are left to answer at eight o'clock tonight, Messick against Hagen Smith, still one win from a first pennant-round berth since 2005

Cleveland arrived at Rate Field with its season reduced to a single afternoon and its batting order, as this paper measured only yesterday, carrying seven hits in sixty-one October at-bats. The response was a nine-run recital. The hosts struck first — Kyle Teel's double cashing Sam Antonacci in the opening inning — and then the third arrived and the famine ended: Steven Kwan lined the tying single, and Jo Adell, with two down, emptied the sacks with a triple past the right fielder — three runs on one swing and a 4-1 lead that was never seriously disputed again.

The afternoon belonged, as Cleveland afternoons will, to José Ramírez. The 34-year-old captain — he of the fractured summer and the aching wrist who told this paper's wire brethren that pain was no excuse — went 2-for-4 with a double, a two-run triple sliced on an 0-2 curveball in front of a diving Grichuk in the eighth, two runs scored, a stolen base, and a gloved robbery at third base that the Chicago crowd heard in silence.8 His teammates have ceased to be surprised. “Why are you surprised? This is what I do,” runs his standing answer, as catcher and outfield alike attested.

The pitching ledger deserves its own paragraph: seven Cleveland arms — Espino briefly, then Griffin brilliantly, seven strikeouts across two and two-thirds for the win, then Armstrong, Cantillo, Gaddis, Herrin and Smith — fanned nineteen White Sox batsmen in nine innings, a smothering the box score renders as six hits and three runs, one of them pushed across by a hit batsman. Chicago's own relay, assembled bullpen-fashion behind the opener Newcomb, was solvent for two innings and ruinous thereafter; Hudson was charged with the third-inning collapse.

So the series stands two games to one for Chicago, and the arithmetic is simple and loud. Game 4 is tonight at eight o'clock Eastern on the South Side, the left-hander Parker Messick (12-9, 2.56, with 193 strikeouts on the season's books) against the left-hander Hagen Smith (3-3, 1.29);10 a fifth game, should Cleveland force it, would be played Saturday by the lake in Cleveland.2 The White Sox remain one victory from a first Championship Series since 2005 — and, as this paper has noted, from a first home playoff clincher since the World Series of 1906. The ghost of that drought now has company in the building: all four of Chicago's October wins this fall were taken on the road, and the home crowd has yet to see one.

THE NINTH MAN IN THE ORDER SPEAKS LOUDEST FOR THE DEEPEST ORDER IN THE LAND — PAGES UNLOADS THE BASES IN THE SEVENTH, MUNCY APPENDS A PARTING SHOT, AND THE ANGELENOS PASS TO A THIRD STRAIGHT CHAMPIONSHIP SERIES: DODGERS 4, BRAVES 1

A game of errors, walks and one wild pitch waits all evening for a single clean swing, and it belongs to the No. 9 hitter — Andy Pages lining a bases-loaded single to center with two out in the seventh for the lead — before Muncy's ninth-inning drive to right, his third of this postseason, closes both the 4-1 verdict and Atlanta's season of eight runs in four October games; Glasnow survives five walks on one hit allowed, Henriquez wins in relief, Díaz seals it, and the Atlantas go to winter while Los Angeles packs for Milwaukee and Sunday

The clinching game at Truist Park was an untidy affair that waited seven innings for someone to put it in order, and it was fitting — perhaps ominous, if you bat leadoff for anyone remaining in this tournament — that the man who did so hits ninth for Los Angeles. With two out and the bases loaded in the seventh of a 1-1 game, Andy Pages lined a single to center that cashed two runs, and the Division Series was, in every sense that matters, concluded on the spot.1

What preceded it was attrition. Atlanta's lone run scored in the first on a wild pitch from Tyler Glasnow, who then walked five men across four and two-thirds innings while allowing precisely one hit — a tightrope act above a canyon that never quite became a plunge. Los Angeles leveled in the second when Max Muncy reached on a Dubón error that let Ohtani cross, one of two Atlanta misplays on the night. Mahle, the Atlanta starter, was excellent and unlucky: six and a third innings, three hits, one earned run, beaten by the seventh-inning inheritance his bullpen could not protect. Muncy supplied the coda in the ninth, a drive over the right-field barrier — his third circuit of this postseason — for the final 4-1.

The Atlanta epitaph is written in the hitting column: three hits on the night, two of them by the blameless Michael Harris II, and eight runs across the four games of the series. The pitching kept every defeat within reach; the batting declined, to the last, to reach. A franchise that pushed the titleholders to a fourth game will spend its winter asking why the lumber never arrived.

Los Angeles, by contrast, advances to a third consecutive Championship Series in pursuit of a third consecutive title, and does so with its October machinery humming in the late innings — Henriquez the winner, Scott the bridge, Díaz the lock for his second save of the round. The itinerary is fixed: Game 1 of the National League Championship Series is Sunday the 11th in Milwaukee, Game 2 Monday, against the Brewers outfit that eliminated San Diego hours later.2 The two clubs met in this very round last October; the rematch the whole league assumed all summer is now a fact of the schedule.

THE WALL AT THE MISSION SHORE GIVES NOTHING BACK — MITCHELL TRIPLES AND SCORES THE GO-AHEAD RUN, THEN LEAPS THE BARRIER'S EDGE TO STEAL MACHADO'S EQUALIZER, AND THE SUDS MEN TAKE THE SERIES WHILE AN OCTOBER ROAD FAMINE DIES AT A DOZEN: BREWERS 3, PADRES 1

One night after this paper measured Milwaukee's twelve straight October road defeats against a mark sixty-two years old, the streak is put to death in the clinching game — Garrett Mitchell authoring the whole verdict with an RBI single in the third, a fifth-inning triple and the tie-breaking run that followed it, and at the last a leaping, fan-jostled catch at the center-field wall that swallows Manny Machado's 406-foot bid to square the eighth; Gasser and Ashby split seven strong innings, Megill closes a three-hitter, the new father Miller throws a scoreless frame in a lost cause, and San Diego's season ends one swing short of extra arguments

Every October series ends on a handful of inches, and the National League's second Division Series ended on the few between Garrett Mitchell's glove and the top of the center-field wall. Eighth inning, Milwaukee ahead 3-1, a man aboard, and Machado met a sinker from Abner Uribe with the full fury of a proud season — 106.7 miles the hour off the bat, a projected 406 feet, Petco Park rising as one to call it even.9 Mitchell drifted back, leapt at the barrier's edge, took a nudge from the reaching crowd — “I'm not quite sure if I got grabbed,” he allowed afterward — and came down with the baseball and, for all practical purposes, the series. “Nice play,” was Machado's verdict. “Should have hit it harder.”

It was Mitchell's game long before the catch. His single cashed Frelick for the first run in the third; after Tatis answered with a drive to center to level it, Mitchell tripled in the fifth and came home on Chourio's single for the lead that never left. Frelick's sacrifice fly added the third run in the sixth. The pitching was a two-man argument settled early: the young Gasser gave four innings and the Tatis run, Aaron Ashby followed with three hitless, and Uribe and Megill — the latter for his second save of the round — carried the three-hitter home. San Diego's offense, so resourceful in the middle games of this series, finished with three hits and the lone Tatis blow.

And so fell a famine of genuine antiquity. As this paper set down only yesterday, Milwaukee had lost twelve consecutive October road games, a run tying a mark sixty-two years in the making; it ends in the most emphatic manner available, a clinching on foreign ground. The Brewers advance to a second consecutive Championship Series, where the Dodgers — their executioners of last autumn — arrive in Milwaukee for Game 1 on Sunday the 11th.2 The first seed in the league will at last play a round with the home advantage it spent six months earning.

For San Diego the ledger closes: a series lost three games to one, a closer restored from the paternity list in time to throw one spotless and irrelevant inning, and a winter of hard questions taken up, as all such questions are, in the colder columns of November.

News Around the League

THE RECKONING DESK: JUDGE BIDS THE COUNTING-HOUSE GO ALL IN — THE CAPTAIN, A SPECTATOR FOR ALL FIVE OCTOBER CONTESTS, SETS THE WINTER'S AGENDA WHILE BOONE KEEPS THE WHEEL

The last strike was scarcely called in the Bronx before the captain convened the winter. Aaron Judge, held out of all five of New York's postseason games by the right calf he had spent two weeks arguing with, delivered a pointed message to the front office: “We're the Yankees... I feel like they should go all in and do what they need to do,” naming no player and sparing no purse. Asked whether the club had gone all in heretofore, he hesitated — “It's tough to say” — before allowing that a winning team every year “is not good enough here in New York.”6

The seventeenth season has now passed since the organization's last championship, and the machinery is creaking audibly. General manager Brian Cashman's contract expires this offseason; manager Aaron Boone, nine years at the helm with a regular-season ledger of 790-565 and one pennant (the 2024 flag, surrendered to Los Angeles in five), has a year remaining, and the grandstands were chanting for his removal even as Grisham swung through the season's final pitch. Judge, for his part, wants Boone kept: “He's our manager. He's running the ship.” Among the prominent men whose papers now come due: Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trent Grisham, and the closer David Bednar.6

The Herald will note, as is its custom when a counting-house pleads its circumstances, that the captain's arithmetic is sound. The purse exists; the question, as ever, is the will to open it.

THE PENNANT DESK: THE FINAL FOUR TAKE THEIR MARKS — MILWAUKEE RECEIVES THE CHAMPIONS SUNDAY IN A SECOND STRAIGHT OCTOBER QUARREL, AND TAMPA BAY AWAITS A GUEST STILL TO BE NAMED

The bracket, so crowded a week ago, is nearly swept clean. In the National League the Championship Series is fixed: Los Angeles at Milwaukee, Game 1 Sunday the 11th, Game 2 Monday the 12th, both in Milwaukee.2 It is a rematch of last autumn's quarrel and a meeting of the league's first and second seeds — the Brewers reach a second consecutive Championship Series; the Dodgers, winners of the last two World Series, a third straight. Milwaukee will remember that its October road famine ended only Wednesday; Los Angeles will remember everything else.

In the American League, Tampa Bay's seat is reserved and the other chair stands empty. The Championship Series opens Monday the 12th at the Rays' dome, against whichever of Cleveland and Chicago survives a Division Series that Chicago leads two games to one with Game 4 on the South Side tonight.23 The Rays, having dispatched New York without the inconvenience of a defeat, are granted four days' rest and the pleasure of watching their next opponent spend its pitching.

The World Series is appointed to begin the 23rd of October, with ground held for a seventh game on the 31st should the quarrel require one.2 The Herald counsels against wasting an evening of it.

THE ALMANAC DESK: FOUR CONTESTS, FOUR VISITORS VICTORIOUS — A THING NEVER BEFORE SEEN IN OCTOBER'S LONG LEDGER

Wednesday's slate deserves a line in the annals apart from its clinchings. Four postseason games were played, and the road team won every one of them — Cleveland at Chicago, Tampa Bay at New York, Los Angeles at Atlanta, Milwaukee at San Diego — and the researchers confirm it had never happened before. Days of four or more postseason games have occurred fifty times, beginning once in the split season of 1981 and yearly since the Division Series arrived in 1995, and never until now had the visitors run the table.7

The opposite feat is on the books twice: the home nines swept four-game days on the 5th of October, 2018, and the 1st of October, 2020 — though the latter, played in the empty ballparks of that strange season, had no crowds to please.7 Wednesday's grandstands, by contrast, were full and went home disappointed in four cities at once, a melancholy quadruple the Herald does not expect to see matched soon.

The moral, if October owes us one: the modern game has made a fiction of the home advantage in its sternest month. Three of the four visitors clinched on foreign lawns; the fourth, Cleveland, saved its season there. The bunting, it appears, is purely decorative.

THE STORK DESK: THE NEW FATHER RETURNS TO A CAUSE PAST SAVING — MILLER, BACK FROM THE CRADLE-SIDE, THROWS A SPOTLESS INNING IN THE EVENING HIS CLUB EXPIRES

A coda to the week's most human story. Mason Miller, the hardest-throwing man in San Diego's employ, was restored from the paternity list Wednesday, his first child safely arrived, and took the ball in a game his club could not afford to lose.1 He gave it his customary best — an inning without a run, two singles stranded — and it mattered not at all, for the Milwaukee men had already banked the lead that ended the Friars' season.

The Herald's readers will recall the arc entire: Monday's number found Miller lined into heartbreak by young Chourio with the bases loaded; Tuesday's found the film men of San Diego declining, twice, to say whether the closer was showing his cards; yesterday's found him departing an elimination game for the birth of his first child, with Peralta summoned to his roster seat. Now the season he left is finished, and the fatherhood he left it for endures. Of the two ledgers, the Herald knows which it would rather hold.

San Diego's winter questions — the aging core, the thin purse, the closer's own approaching market — are questions for another number. Today the paper records only that a man kept both of his appointments in the same week, and that neither the ballclub nor the baby can claim he shorted them an inning.

A rare economy tonight: one contest only, Cleveland at Chicago at eight o'clock Eastern, with a season on one side of the scale and a pennant-round berth on the other. Friday the calendar rests entirely; Saturday holds a fifth game by the lake should Cleveland force it tonight; Sunday the National League's Championship Series opens in Milwaukee, and Monday the American's at Tampa Bay, with the World Series appointed for the 23rd.2 The Herald, having watched four road clubs strip four home crowds of their evening in a single day, offers the grandstands of the South Side its sincerest wishes and no guarantees. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: TWO CAPS TIP ACROSS SIXTY FEET, AND THE SECOND SITTING GOES TO THE VISITORS — YAMAMOTO FANS TEN THROUGH SEVEN, KIKÉ AND FREEMAN STRIKE TWICE IN THREE BATTERS OF THE FOURTH, AND ATLANTA STANDS ONE DEFEAT FROM WINTER: DODGERS 3, BRAVES 1
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 91 · Wednesday, the Seventh of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 2 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

TWO CAPS TIP ACROSS SIXTY FEET, AND THE SECOND SITTING GOES TO THE VISITORS — YAMAMOTO FANS TEN THROUGH SEVEN, KIKÉ AND FREEMAN STRIKE TWICE IN THREE BATTERS OF THE FOURTH, AND ATLANTA STANDS ONE DEFEAT FROM WINTER: DODGERS 3, BRAVES 1

Before a pitch is thrown the two aces exchange tipped caps across the Truist Park lawn, and for three innings the rematch of the August masterpiece honors its billing — six strikeouts apiece, nothing scored — until Enrique Hernández turns on Sale for a two-run four-bagger and Freeman, a month's drought lately behind him, clears the barrier two batters later; Yamamoto, in his first appearance since recording the final outs of last autumn's seventh game, carries a postseason-best ten strikeouts through seven innings of one-run ball, Díaz holds the ninth for his first save in nearly two months, and the champions stand one victory from a third consecutive Championship Series while Atlanta's offense, seven runs in three games, runs out of evenings to find itself

The engagement opened with a courtesy. Before a pitch had been thrown Tuesday night at Truist Park, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Chris Sale tipped their caps to one another across the diamond — two craftsmen acknowledging the appointment this paper's Tuesday number called the hinge of the whole quarrel.3 For three innings the bill was honored to the letter: six strikeouts apiece and nothing scored, the first postseason game to open so since Kershaw and deGrom traded ciphers in the first game of the 2015 Division Series.4 The 42,420 in the seats had every reason to expect the sequel to run like the original — the 1-0 shutout Sale pitched against this same club in this same yard on the 27th of August, when Yamamoto allowed one run and took the loss for his trouble.3 Then came the fourth inning, and with it the oldest chapter in the Los Angeles October hymnal.

Andy Pages singled, and Enrique Hernández — the October familiar whom his own teammates discuss in tones of baffled admiration — turned on Sale and dropped a two-run drive over the left-field wall, the 17th postseason home run of his career. The man homers once in every 19.5 October trips to the plate, against once in every 31.7 the summer long. Two batters later Freeman, who before Monday had gone better than a month without an extra-base hit, found the right-center seats for his second home run in as many games and the 18th of his playoff life. "I wish there was a recipe for that so we can all take it from him," said Freeman of his colleague's annual transformation. "He's incredible. He shows up when you need him." Sale's evening closed after five innings and seven hits, three runs in all, and Atlanta had lost behind its ace for the first time since the 21st of August.4

Yamamoto wanted no more. The splitter working from the first, he retired 12 of his first 14 men, and when Atlanta loaded the bases with one out in the fifth, the damage was held to a groundout — struck by Baldwin, who in the August meeting had supplied the lone run off Yamamoto by home run, as these columns recalled only yesterday, and now supplied Tuesday's lone Atlanta run by humbler means. Ten strikeouts across seven innings made a postseason high for a man pitching for the first time since he closed the seventh game of last year's World Series; he is the third Japanese-born pitcher to reach double figures in an October game, after Ohtani and Kuroda, and the first Dodger to pair seven innings and ten strikeouts with one run or fewer since Snell in last autumn's Wild Card round. His club has now won 10 of the 11 postseason games in which he has pitched. "He was attacking us and putting the ball where he wanted to put it," testified the Atlanta second baseman Albies. "I mean, it was really rough." The pitcher's own account was briefer: "I was able to carry that feel into today's game."3 Scott took the eighth without a run, and the ninth went to Edwin Díaz — the reclamation project whose mid-game trumpets this paper heard Monday — who banked his first save in nearly two months, having recorded but three all summer after the 7th of April.8

The manager Roberts pronounced the method: "We played tonight like an elimination game."3 The arithmetic explains the urgency and now rewards it: in best-of-five series standing one game apiece, the winner of the third has taken the series 48 times in 67, and clubs carrying a two-games-to-one lead into a fourth game on the road have gone through 26 times in 37, twenty of those clinchings coming in the fourth game itself.3 Atlanta's remaining case rests on bats that have produced seven runs in three games: Baldwin bats .130 for the October, Olson .174, and Acuña — moved to designated hitter 90 minutes before the first pitch to spare his right knee — .143 without an extra-base hit since the 19th of September. "Those guys have been our aircraft carriers all year," insisted the manager Weiss. "They're always one at-bat away from changing a game." Los Angeles has questions of its own carried lightly: Ohtani, dropped to fifth in the order for the first time in six years, went hitless again — "he's going to come to life. It will happen," shrugged Roberts — and Rojas left the eighth inning with pain in his lower back.43 The fourth game goes this evening at 6 o'clock Eastern at Truist Park, Glasnow opposite Mahle; should Atlanta force a fifth, it would be played Friday at 8 at Dodger Stadium.28

The Postseason Card

NO MILLER, NO MOREJON, NO MATTER — KING RETURNS TWO DAYS AFTER A FIVE-INNING START TO SEIZE THE LAST SIX OUTS, BOGAERTS SLAMS THE GATE WITH A GAME-ENDING DOUBLE PLAY, AND MILWAUKEE'S TWELFTH STRAIGHT OCTOBER ROAD DEFEAT TIES A MARK TWO-AND-SIXTY YEARS IN THE MAKING: PADRES 4, BREWERS 3

San Diego's third early two-run lead of the series is erased a third time, Cronenworth's first-pitch answer off Romero restores the advantage for good, and Bogaerts manufactures the decisive run with his spikes — leaping clear of a broken bat on his way to third and racing home when the rookie Pratt bounces the throw — before Michael King, who gave five innings and 72 pitches in Sunday's second game, walks the tying and go-ahead men aboard in the ninth and watches Yelich's 107-mph liner die in Bogaerts' glove; the Mission nine, their closer called to the cradle and their best left-handed reliever shelved by a weary shoulder, force a fourth game at 10 o'clock Eastern tonight, while Milwaukee — still ahead two games to one — has now lost twelve consecutive postseason road games, equaling a record the Senators and Twins spent 62 years assembling

San Diego came to its elimination evening missing the two best arms in its bullpen — Miller summoned to the paternity rolls hours before the first pitch, as the Stork Desk reports above, and Morejon shelved by a weary shoulder — and played before 47,708 at Petco Park the third consecutive game of this series to be decided by a single run. No postseason series had opened with three one-run games since the 2021 Championship Series, and only thirteen on record have ever done it.56 For the third time running the home nine banked an early two-run lead, this one in the third on Tatis' run-scoring groundout and Machado's single; for the third time running Milwaukee erased it, Contreras lifting his second home run of the series in the fourth and Chourio's sacrifice fly squaring the account in the fifth — though only after Turang had bounced out with the bases full in the top of that inning, the costliest of a night of strandings. Cronenworth answered Romero's first pitch of the bottom half with the go-ahead drive into the right-field seats, and the decisive run scored in the sixth on pure larceny: Bogaerts singled, took second on a wild pitch, broke for third as Andujar's broken-bat bouncer and half the bat itself spun toward the rookie shortstop Pratt, leapt clear of both in stride — and raced home when Pratt's hurried throw found the dirt. "You can make excuses about everything, but I fielded the ball and I threw the ball in the dirt," said Pratt. "I cost us a run."6

Milwaukee's reply made it 4-3 in the seventh, Yelich lining a single to center to cash Contreras — snapping a drought of nineteen postseason games without a run batted in, reaching back to the opening game of the 2018 pennant round — and then the evening became Michael King's. The San Diego ace, 72 pitches into Sunday's second game, had presented himself in the manager's office in the afternoon: "He came in the office today and said I'm available," Stammen related. King paced the bullpen through the seventh, breezed the eighth, and in the ninth walked Contreras and Turang with one out before Yelich lined his 40th pitch — 107.1 miles the hour off the bat, an expected average of .630 by the instruments — directly at Bogaerts, who scooped the one-hop, stepped on second, and fired to first for the ending. It was King's first save in more than four years; he is the sixteenth pitcher since the save became official in 1969 to start a game of five innings and record a save in the same postseason series, and the first since Buehler in the 2024 World Series — the same Buehler who takes the ball for San Diego tonight. "I have bullets in my arm that I don't want to save," said King. "You're in an elimination game, you want everybody to be all-in on it. Not just me included. We have a bunch of dogs down there that are all-in."5

For Milwaukee the loss carried an antique echo: twelve consecutive postseason defeats on the road, tying the dubious record the Senators and Twins assembled across 62 years and one change of address, 1925 to 1987. The franchise stands 6-24 away from home in October play and has not won on the road since the third game of the 2018 Championship Series — a club, its men note, with exactly one survivor from that evening. "I mean, this team has one person playing from 2018," said Yelich, who is that person. "So that really has no effect on this group." The manager Murphy entered a plea for the ancestors — "I wouldn't beat up the old Brewers if you don't mind," says he, noting that all but one of the clubs that handed Milwaukee those twelve went on to the World Series — and the reliever Ashby supplied the banner for tonight: "It's like we've got 40 guys versus 50,000. That's a cool feeling." Merrill, it should be entered, twice robbed the visitors with his glove in center, beginning with Chourio's first-inning drive to the wall. The fourth game goes at 10 o'clock Eastern at Petco Park, Milwaukee's starter unannounced against Buehler; a fifth, should San Diego force it, would be played Friday at half past four in Milwaukee.62

News Around the League

THE GAUNTLET DESK: FOUR CONTESTS, FOUR POSSIBLE CODAS — THE YEAR'S LAST FOUR-GAME DAY RUNS FROM THE SOUTH SIDE AT FOUR O'CLOCK TO THE PACIFIC AT TEN, AND EVERY ONE OF THEM COULD END A SERIES

Mark the date: today is the final day of 2026 with four games on the card, and each of the four could close a Division Series.8 The order of ceremonies, by the forward ledger: Cleveland at Chicago at 4 o'clock Eastern, Espino opposite Newcomb, the White Sox two games up; Los Angeles at Atlanta at 6, Glasnow against Mahle, the champions leading two games to one; Tampa Bay at New York at 8, Martinez against Fried, the Rays likewise two up; and Milwaukee at San Diego at 10, the Brewers' starter unannounced against Buehler, Milwaukee a game from the pennant round.21

For Chicago the afternoon is a homecoming besides — the whole of this White Sox October has been played on the road, and the South Side has not hosted a playoff game since 2021. Mr. Leitch of MLB.com ventures that the yard now called Rate Field has not known an atmosphere to match this one since the first two games of the 2005 World Series, the opener of which was attended by the Chicago-born churchman who, twenty years on, would be elevated as Pope Leo XIV. The scrapbook counsels humility all the same: in 2008 and again in 2021 the club came home down two games, won once, and was eliminated in the fourth game. The present edition — four October victories without a defeat, every one of them taken in somebody else's yard — aims at the franchise's fourth Championship Series and, as this paper's columns have lately rehearsed, a first home series-clinching victory in 120 years.8

THE STORK DESK: THE BULLPEN'S GRANDEST ARM ANSWERS A HIGHER SUMMONS — MILLER LEAVES AN ELIMINATION GAME FOR THE CRADLE, PERALTA TAKES HIS ROSTER SEAT, AND SAN DIEGO AWAITS TWO ARRIVALS AT ONCE

The paternity rolls, whose first October call this paper entered Sunday, have now claimed the heaviest arm in the San Diego bullpen. Mason Miller telephoned the club early Tuesday afternoon: his wife, Jordan, had gone into labor. The closer — a 1.67 figure across 66 regular-season appearances, and lately the subject of the tipping inquest these columns conducted Tuesday — was placed on the paternity list hours before an elimination game, the left-hander Wandy Peralta taking his seat on the series roster.7 The statute allows an absence of one to three days; the club anticipates its man back for tonight's fourth game — "That's what we're anticipating," said the pitching instructor Niebla — and failing that, for a fifth game Friday, when by rule it must be Peralta who gives way. His teammates waved him off without a murmur. "We have his back," said Tatis. "Let him have his family time right now." France, himself called to the same rolls in September, allowed: "I know it's a hard thing to balance, but he's doing the right thing." The stork has thus visited the San Diego club three times this season — France in September, Buehler on the eve of the third game, and now Miller.7

The evening disclosed a second subtraction more quietly. Morejon, the bullpen's best left hand, has been nursing fatigue in his throwing shoulder — "stickiness," the manager Stammen called it — and though he played catch and even took the bullpen mound before the game, the club declined to push him. How San Diego lines up behind Buehler tonight is, by the manager's own admission, contingent on both men; the club professes not to know.5

THE INFIRMARY DESK: SEVEN HITS IN ONE-AND-SIXTY AT-BATS — CLEVELAND'S COLD ORDER FOLLOWS ITS CAPTAIN'S FRACTURED SUMMER TO CHICAGO, WHERE RAMÍREZ HAS STRUCK MORE HOME RUNS THAN ANY VISITOR NOW PLAYING

Cleveland's predicament, reduced to a line of agate: the order has gone 7 for 61 in this series — a .115 mark — with eight hitless at-bats when a runner stood in scoring position, and José Ramírez, the franchise's dearest son, has yet to record a hit. The fuller explanation resides in his left wrist. Ramírez fractured the hamate bone on the 13th of June and returned in five weeks and a day — quicker than the surgeons asked — and the power never followed: twelve home runs and a .688 OPS across 125 games, his poorest figures since 2015, with two home runs in his final 53 games. The pain, he has acknowledged, will keep until winter, and the strength is not expected whole before spring training. "It has been difficult," said Ramírez. "There are days when it might feel better, and others when it feels worse. But that is no excuse. The mentality is to go out and compete and try to win."9

The manager Vogt declines the alibi on his man's behalf and the despair besides: "He's not 100 percent and hasn't been since June, but he's giving us everything he has, and we all know José's one swing of the bat away from getting it going... I have a feeling he's going to come through for us." And the venue argues for the feeling: Ramírez has hit 23 home runs at Rate Field as a visitor, the most of any man now active and second in all history to Cabrera's 26. Cleveland, two defeats into the series with none to spare, will learn by suppertime whether the one swing arrives in time.9

THE ARCHIVES DESK: AT TWO GAMES DOWN, NEW YORK TAKES ITS SCRAPBOOK OFF THE SHELF — THE FLIP OF 2001 AND THE RALLY OF 2017 ARE READ ALOUD IN THE BRONX, WHERE FRIED AND THE UNANSWERABLE RICE MUST HOLD THE LINE TONIGHT

No franchise keeps a thicker scrapbook, and at two games down the Bronx has turned to the comfortable pages. Mr. Lupica of MLB.com directs the anxious reader to the 13th of October, 2001 — third game of a Division Series against an Oakland club that, like these Rays, had bettered New York's season record and taken the first two games — when Jeter crossed the whole infield to collect an overthrown relay and backhanded his famous flip to Posada, the runner Giambi beaten by a step, the game held 1-0, the series in time won entire. Beside it sits 2017, when the club climbed from the same 0-2 grave against Cleveland. The less comfortable page — last October's 0-2 against Toronto, never answered — the readership declines to open.10

The case for hope bats left-handed. Rice is hitting .467 for the October with four home runs and eight runs batted in through four games, carrying the offense as he carried it through the captain Judge's absent summer; and the starting pitching has committed no crime, Cole and Schlittler having yielded three earned runs between them in the series while the defense kicked away the second game behind them. Tonight the ball goes to Fried, who opened the Wild Card round with six innings of one-run ball against Boston. The sober entry on the facing page: Tampa Bay has beaten New York nine times in fifteen meetings this season, puts every ball in play, and does not beat itself. The manager Boone states the assignment without ornament: "We've got the chance to do something great... We've responded to difficult times all season. Now we gotta do it again." And, more plainly still: "We gotta get a game."10

The National League supplied both of the day-prior entries and left both of its quarrels standing two games to one — Los Angeles a win from the pennant round after the aces' rematch went to Yamamoto, San Diego alive by the width of a double play. Now comes the densest page left on the calendar: four contests today, every one a possible ending — Cleveland at Chicago at 4 o'clock Eastern, Los Angeles at Atlanta at 6, Tampa Bay at New York at 8, Milwaukee at San Diego at 10 — and no day hereafter holds more than two, the Championship Series opening the 11th of the month in the National League and the 12th in the American.2 Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: ELEVEN STRIKEOUTS BUY CLEVELAND FIVE INNINGS AND NOT AN OUT MORE — VOGT LIFTS WILLIAMS AT HIS EIGHT-AND-NINETIETH PITCH, THE SIXTH COMES APART IN RELIEF, AND MONTGOMERY'S TWO-RUN DOUBLE SENDS CHICAGO HOME NEEDING ONE: WHITE SOX 4, GUARDIANS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — the pennants are being decided, and spring must wait its turn.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 90 · Tuesday, the Sixth of October, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 2 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

ELEVEN STRIKEOUTS BUY CLEVELAND FIVE INNINGS AND NOT AN OUT MORE — VOGT LIFTS WILLIAMS AT HIS EIGHT-AND-NINETIETH PITCH, THE SIXTH COMES APART IN RELIEF, AND MONTGOMERY'S TWO-RUN DOUBLE SENDS CHICAGO HOME NEEDING ONE: WHITE SOX 4, GUARDIANS 3

The hardest arm on the lakefront fans eleven with 18 pitches at 100 miles the hour or better, hands a one-run lead to his bullpen after a leadoff single in the sixth, and watches it burn — Sabrowski walking the pinch-hitter Grichuk on four pitches, uncorking a wild pitch, and standing one short fly from escape when Braden Montgomery lines a two-run double the opposite way; Sean Burke retires 13 in a row in bulk relief, Grant Taylor survives Adell's first-pitch triple to close the 4-3 verdict, and the Pale Hose — who trailed for the first time all postseason after an unearned two-run first — fly home with four October victories, all of them taken on the road, one win from a first Championship Series since 2005 and a first home playoff clincher since the World Series of 1906

For five innings and one batter Monday evening, the argument belonged to the heaviest artillery this paper promised. Gavin Williams was everything Cleveland's predicament required: eleven strikeouts, five of them in unbroken succession from the end of the first inning to the top of the third — no Cleveland pitcher had ever done that in October — and 18 pitches at 100 miles the hour or better, tying Emmanuel Clase's franchise mark of the whole tracking era. He became but the third Cleveland man to reach double figures in strikeouts in a postseason game, one shy of Charles Nagy's record twelve of 1996, and he carried a 2-1 lead into the sixth.5 The lead itself had been staked in the first, and not honestly earned: Kwan's leadoff single off the opener Kay, a pass to Ramírez, an intentional walk around Adell — and then Lowe's comebacker to the second relayman Newcomb, whose throw sailed past Murakami at first while two runs crossed. Thus did the White Sox trail in a 2026 postseason game for the first time, their streak expiring at 27 innings, 24 of them led, as this paper's columns had counted them.3

Then came the hinge on which Cleveland's whole October may yet swing. Miguel Vargas — the one Chicago batsman giving Williams honest trouble, with two walks already to his evening — led off the sixth with a single to left, and the manager Vogt, his starter at 98 pitches, went to the bullpen. "If he has to face two more hitters, now you're running him up to 110, 115," Vogt reasoned afterward. "It was the right time to get him out of there. He pitched his backside off. Just unfortunate we were not able to get the result." The left-hander Sabrowski, nearly untouchable since August, chose this night to have nothing: Murakami's groundout moved the runner, Grichuk walked on four pitches, a wild pitch advanced the pair, and after Pham's short fly to left brought escape within a single out, Braden Montgomery — a rookie who has labored all season from the right side — lined a two-run double down the right-field line. Gaddis relieved and was greeted by Meidroth's run-scoring single, and a 2-1 Cleveland lead had become a 4-2 Chicago one, five batters wide. "Just lack of control," said Sabrowski. "It's unfortunate. It was a pretty big part of the game, and I let a lot of guys down."5

The relay that followed was the one this paper sketched in Monday's columns, run precisely to the drawing. Sean Burke, the staff's ace recast as a man of bulk, gave five innings and a third on one hit and one run, striking out six and at one stretch retiring 13 in succession — tied for the second-longest such run by a reliever in any postseason game, behind only Bumgarner's 14 in the seventh game of the 2014 World Series.4 "Tip your cap to Burke, what an unbelievable performance," ruled Vogt. "He was mixing and matching, criss-crossing away, criss-crossing in." Kwan testified that the fastball "just had a little extra life on it." Murakami's fourth-inning single had meanwhile cashed Teel for Chicago's first run, and when Burke yielded a two-out single to DeLauter in the eighth, the closer Taylor — twelve outs of save on Saturday, seven pitches wanted Monday — was greeted rudely: Adell's first-pitch triple to the left-center gap, a foot or two of wall shy of a tying home run, scored DeLauter to make it 4-3. Lowe then lined to left, where Antonacci ran the ball down at full stretch, and Taylor's ninth went three up, three down for the save.3

So Chicago, which has not played a home game this October, carries two victories to Rate Field, where Wednesday's third game goes at 4 o'clock Eastern before a sellout that will wear the Blackout in broad daylight. The arithmetic is stern for the hosts-to-be-visitors: clubs ahead two games to none in a best-of-five have gone through 83 times in 93, and clubs that took the first two on the road under the present format 17 times in 19; the last side to climb from such a hole was the 2017 Yankees — at Cleveland's own expense, the Guardians will not need reminding, though they may prefer the omen that they played better on the road (44-37) than at home this summer.36 Cleveland had named no starter by press time — Bibee, Griffin, and Cantillo, whose September behind the opener Espino ran 15 scoreless innings with 17 strikeouts, are the candidates, and Williams himself volunteers for the bullpen on one day's rest — while Chicago's likeliest man is the rookie Smith, author of 5 2/3 scoreless innings this postseason.6 The stakes on the South Side want no embroidery: one victory sends the White Sox to a first Championship Series since the 11-and-1 champions of 2005, and would seal the club's first home playoff clincher since the 14th of October, 1906, when they beat the Cubs at South Side Park for the title — 120 years gone. "It's going to be unbelievable. Those fans deserve it," said Taylor. "They have been with us for three years of 100 losses." Cleveland's answer came from Kwan, and it was steady as ever: "There's no panic button. We're not trying to do too much."3

The Postseason Card

THE GLOVES OF GOTHAM GIVE FOUR TIMES AND THE FIFTH INNING COLLECTS IN FULL — RICE'S PAIR OF CIRCUIT CLOUTS STANDS ALONE AGAINST A RALLY OF SINGLES AND SHOE LEATHER: GULF COAST CLUB 5, PINSTRIPES 2

The league's most un-strikeout-able order plays its signature hand — Aranda's single and Caminero's 112.4-mile double opening a four-run fifth finished by Simpson's legs, a stolen base, another New York misplay, and Palacios' two-run single on the eighth pitch of his turn — while Schlittler, the presumptive Cy Young choice of the scribes, is wrung for the fewest strikeouts of his career, two; Ben Rice homers twice on changeups and becomes the first Yankee ever to post two multi-homer games in a single postseason, Jones' fly ball strikes the B-ring catwalk and is patiently caught, and the top seed flies north two games to none — Game 3 Wednesday at eight in the Bronx, Fried against Martinez, with New York's season on the board

The Rays were asked before the game for their plan against Cam Schlittler, the young road warrior whose new curveball this paper admired only yesterday, and the shortstop Walls gave the answer of a man with nothing to hide: "Just kind of do what we've been doing all year." What they have done all year is strike out less than any club in the majors and put the ball upon the ground until something gives, and Monday night at Tropicana Field, before a sold-out house of 40,226, what gave was the New York infield. The first inning yielded a run without an earned deed in it — McMahon fumbling Díaz's grounder, Aranda singling, and Chisholm throwing away the force at second as Díaz crossed — one of three New York errors in that frame alone and four on the night, charged to four different gloves. Schlittler, for only the third time in his young career, finished his first two innings without a strikeout.7

Ben Rice answered alone. In the fourth he turned on a Peralta changeup — a pitch that had yielded no extra-base hit since the right-hander crossed to Tampa Bay — and found the right-field seats to square the account; in the eighth he did it again, off a Seymour changeup, and the scribes' ledger opened wide. Rice is the first man in the franchise's 61 postseason appearances to post two multi-homer games in a single October, and the first player in all postseason history to do it within his club's first four games; his five home runs in his first ten postseason games trail only Bernie Williams' six among Yankees, and his four this October tie Gehrig's 1928 for the second-most in the club's first four games of an autumn, behind Stanton's five of 2020. He is also, the instruments attest, the first man since the tracking began to hit two changeups out in a single postseason game.8 Between his salvos the game was settled: Booser wriggled New York's bases-loaded fifth shut, and in the home half Aranda singled, Caminero doubled at 112.4 miles the hour, Hicks grounded a run home, Simpson beat a ball that the shortstop Lombard could not corral, stole second, and watched DeLuca reach on Lombard's error before Palacios — second on the club this season with 31 two-out runs batted in — lined a two-run single up the middle on the eighth pitch of the turn. Four runs, one inning, scarcely a ball struck hard but one. "Constant pressure, constant long at-bats," said the manager Cash. "It's our M.O. all season long."7

The evening's curiosity arrived in the second, when Jones' towering fly struck the B-ring catwalk beneath the dome's roof and hung an age before Mesa settled under it for the out — a lawful catch under the house rules, the higher two rings being in play, and the second piece of October architecture to side with the home nine in three days, the roof cable of Milwaukee having lately confiscated France's home run in these columns. Boone came out to inquire and was shown the statute.9 The fuller indictment of his club wants no catwalk: shut out on one hit in the opener, undone by its own gloves in the second game, New York has scored two runs in 18 innings of this series while the Tampa Bay relief corps proper has been needed for but seven of 54 outs. "We've got to get ourselves up off the mat," said Boone.10

The remedy must be found at home, where the arithmetic grants little: clubs up two games to none in a best-of-five have advanced 83 times in 93, and home winners of the first two under the present format 33 times in 36. Game 3 goes Wednesday at eight o'clock at Yankee Stadium, and the pitching is the hosts' best case: Fried, 5-1 at a 1.81 figure in seven career starts against Tampa Bay and sharp against Boston in the Wild Card round, against the veteran Martinez, a first-time All-Star whose club won 22 of his 31 starts and who held New York to three runs across 12 innings in the Bronx this summer. New York took four of six from the Rays at home this season — but the guests have already corked champagne in that building once this autumn, having clinched the East there on the 22nd of September, and the captain Judge, whose exclusion from these rolls this paper recorded Saturday, remains a spectator still.10

News Around the League

THE ARMS DESK: THE DUEL OF AUGUST IS GRANTED A SECOND SITTING — SALE AGAINST YAMAMOTO AT SIX O'CLOCK IN GEORGIA, THE SERIES SQUARE AND THE THIRD GAME, BY THE LONG LEDGER, THE HINGE OF THE WHOLE QUARREL

The engagement this paper's Monday number announced — the aces unsheathed at last — holds for this evening at Truist Park, and it arrives with a rehearsal already in the books. On the 27th of August these same two men met in this same yard and played a 1-0 masterpiece: Chris Sale a five-hit shutout of the Dodgers, Yoshinobu Yamamoto one run across 6 1/3 innings and the loss for his trouble. Sale, 37 years old, finished the summer with the game's third-best figure at 2.16 — a 1.96 mark over his final 24 starts — and opened this October by holding Philadelphia to three runs over 6 1/3 in the Wild Card round; he was held back from the second game because he had recorded the final four outs of the Wild Card clincher. Yamamoto, the reigning hero of the World Series, makes his first appearance of this postseason carrying a 0.87 WHIP, second among all qualified starters.11

The counting-men assign tonight its full weight: in best-of-five series standing one game apiece, the winner of the third has claimed the series 48 times in 67. The bullpens behind the aces are unevenly provisioned — Atlanta has Iglesias, Suarez, and Lee rested but must do without Fuentes and Kerr, both past 40 pitches Sunday, while Los Angeles returns nearly whole, the rookie Sasaki's 36 pitches the lone question. As for the bats: Harris, 8 for 20 this October, carries Atlanta's order; Acuña (3 for 18 without an extra-base hit) and Olson (3 for 19, seven strikeouts) have yet to join him; Freeman, 3 for 7 with a home run in the series, looks repaired; and Baldwin's leadoff blast accounted for the only run Yamamoto allowed in the August meeting. First pitch at six o'clock.11

THE BRINK DESK: MILWAUKEE CARRIES TWO GAMES AND A PLAIN-SPOKEN STARTER TO THE MISSION SHORE — MAY, THE DEADLINE PRIZE WHO CALLS HIS OWN AUTUMN FRANKLY, AGAINST PIVETTA, FIVE MONTHS MENDED, AT HALF PAST NINE

The National's other quarrel resumes at Petco Park with San Diego's season reduced to a single sentence, supplied by the second baseman Cronenworth: "Win-or-go-home games from here on out, so yeah, we have no choice." Milwaukee hands the ball to Dustin May, its highest-priced freight of the Trade Deadline, whose candor has outrun his results — three earned runs over his first 13 Milwaukee innings, then a 1-2, 7.61 slide across his final eight turns, of which the man himself testified: "It sucks to be sucking right now." The club's wager rests on the fuller ledger: a 3.14 figure in 16 career games against the Friars, and a 1.23 mark in his three starts against them this season. San Diego answers with Nick Pivetta, who lost nearly five months to a flexor strain and has been excellent since his September return — a 1.64 figure across five starts — and whose ugly career number against Milwaukee, 8.76, traces nearly whole to one rookie afternoon of 2017.12

The arithmetic of relief favors the visitors besides: Milwaukee's bullpen has thrown nine scoreless innings in this series, with Megill, Uribe, and Ashby rested by the travel day and the fresh starters Gasser, Drohan, and Harrison standing behind May should the leash run short. San Diego's one reinforcement is a familiar name — Buehler, restored Monday from the paternity rolls whose visit from the stork this paper entered Sunday, and available in relief. Among the bats, Chourio's 15 career postseason runs batted in stand one shy of Braun's franchise mark, while France has opened this October 7 for 15 — with a fair claim, these columns have conceded, to eight and a home run besides, the roof at American Family Field having ruled otherwise. Milwaukee, it bears noting, won 42 games in come-from-behind fashion this summer, tied for fifth most in the league — and has now added two more in October. First pitch at half past nine.12

THE INQUEST DESK: WAS THE CLOSER SHOWING HIS CARDS? MILLER PLEADS COMMAND, NOT TELLS — AND SAN DIEGO'S MEN OF FILM, ASKED TWICE, DECLINE TWICE TO SAY

No topic buzzed louder at San Diego's off-day workout than whether Mason Miller, in the ninth inning this paper chronicled Monday, was tipping his pitches. The internet's magistrates have produced their exhibits: still images suggesting the closer's hand sat more visible out of the glove on his fastballs, and film of Frelick, leading off second, touching his neck before the 1-2 slider that Chourio declined with the season's composure. "That just seemed like a really confident take," Miller allowed of the pitch, though he holds the larger charge unproven and beside the point: "I just don't think it had anything to do with the walks. I also have a hard time believing I just magically started doing it... If you execute pitches, you're still going to get guys out." The batsman Sánchez, for his part, swore ignorance — "I don't know if he was tipping or not. Seriously, I don't" — while the Milwaukee manager Murphy delivered a connoisseur's lecture on the art itself: "Where they stand, if their mouth is open or closed, eyes are down, head is up... Big breath. Small breath. There's so many ways to give away a pitch." Asked plainly whether his club had something, Murphy observed only that the practice "is happening" in today's game — and no club mid-series ever says more.13

The San Diego manager Stammen, twice invited to deny a tell, twice declined, pleading instead a crew "dedicated to that every single day" — and offered the more prosaic diagnosis: Miller's trouble arrives chiefly in his second inning of work, and the six-out ask may be retired for the balance of the round. Miller himself sees no cause to renovate: "It kind of seems like a bad time to try to change everything, too." The Herald notes merely that he may be handed the ball tonight with the season in his palm, and that October is a poor month for unanswered questions.13

THE AWARDS DESK: TWENTY NAMES POSTED FOR THE AARON PRIZE — A PANEL OF LEGENDS AND THE PUBLIC'S FRANCHISE OPEN THROUGH THE TWELFTH, WITH THE VERDICTS SEALED UNTIL NOVEMBER

The league Monday posted its finalists for the Hank Aaron Award, the honor for each league's finest regular-season batsman, and the Herald reports the ballot as a ballot: winners will be named the 11th of November at the MLB Awards in Las Vegas, and until then no man has won anything. The American's ten: Alonso of Baltimore, Alvarez of Houston, Arozarena of Seattle, Caminero and Díaz of Tampa Bay, Contreras of Boston, Greene of Detroit, Rice of New York, Vargas of Chicago, and Witt of Kansas City. The National's: Abrams of Washington, Bauers of Milwaukee, Crow-Armstrong of Chicago, De La Cruz and Stewart of Cincinnati, Ohtani of Los Angeles — thrice the holder, 2023 through 2025 — Olson of Atlanta, Schwarber of Philadelphia, Tatis of San Diego, and Walker of St. Louis. The electors are a bench of legends — Jeter, Ortiz, Pujols, Griffey, Chipper Jones, Pedro Martínez, Smoltz, Bench, Biggio, and Murray — and the public may cast its own votes through noon of the 12th.14

The reader with one eye on the bracket will note the resonance: eight of the twenty finalists are still at their labors in the Division Series — Caminero, Díaz, Rice, and Vargas in the American's two quarrels, Bauers, Ohtani, Olson, and Tatis in the National's — and three of them, Rice, Vargas, and Caminero, spent Monday evening adding to the testimony, as the columns above attest.14

THE JURISPRUDENCE DESK: ROBERTS REVOKES A BATSMAN'S RIGHT OF APPEAL — PAGES, AMONG THE LEAGUE'S LEAST SUCCESSFUL PETITIONERS, IS TOLD TO TAP HIS HELMET NO MORE

The machine's new jurisprudence, whose first-season audit these columns entered Saturday, has produced its first October disbarment. Andy Pages, the Los Angeles center fielder, spent a challenge in the second inning of the series opener on a 2-2 pitch that the instruments placed 2.6 inches above the bottom of the zone — comfortably a strike — and the manager Roberts has now withdrawn the privilege entirely. "We talked about obviously a lot this year with Andy's success rate or lack thereof," said Roberts. "I did have a conversation today. So, yeah, we've managed that one going forward." The figures argue the manager's side: among 182 batsmen with ten or more challenges this season, Pages ranked 142nd in overturns against expectation while spending the 33rd-most challenges, and after a clubhouse address on the subject during an August losing streak he did not challenge again all summer. Roberts was at pains to call the policy a tailored one — "it's not a one-size-fits-all situation," says he, professing full faith in Betts's eye for the outside corner — and the club at large rated a respectable challenger, its 51 percent success standing tied for eighth. But October, as Philadelphia's game-ending helmet tap lately demonstrated and as this paper then observed, is no month for a losing petition.15

Two contests on the Tuesday tables, and the American League wrote the same sentence twice: the visitor won, the favorite's yard fell silent, and both series now stand two games to none — Chicago over Cleveland, Tampa Bay over New York, each leader needing one. Tonight the National answers with its third chapters, Los Angeles at Atlanta at six o'clock with Sale opposite Yamamoto, and Milwaukee at San Diego at half past nine with a sweep in prospect and a season in the balance. The morrow returns the American to the stage — Cleveland at Chicago at four o'clock, Tampa Bay at New York at eight — with the National's fourth games to follow in the same evening as needed; and beyond stand the pennant rounds, the National's Championship Series opening the eleventh of the month and the American's the twelfth, by the league's forward ledger.2 Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
